m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Open Microsoft MakeCode for micro:bit in a browser and create a named project.
  • Point to each part of a micro:bit and say whether it is an input or an output.
  • Find the toolbox, the workspace, the simulator, and the Download button.
  • Paste a MakeCode JavaScript program from this course and see it turn into blocks.

The BBC micro:bit is a complete computer on a board about 5 cm by 4 cm. It has 25 red LEDs, two buttons, a motion sensor, a compass, a thermometer, and a radio, and the V2 version adds a speaker, a microphone, and a touch-sensitive logo. In this course you will turn it into a name badge, a reaction-time game, a step counter, a compass, and radio messengers.

You don't need to own one. Every program in this course runs in Microsoft MakeCode, a free editor that works in your web browser. MakeCode includes a simulator: a virtual micro:bit on the screen that runs your code, with buttons you can click and sensors you can drag. Nothing to install, no account, no cost.

#Two ways through the course

Pick the one that matches what you have. You can switch at any time, because the same project file works on both.

What you need Simulator only With a real board
A computer or Chromebook with a current browser yes yes
A BBC micro:bit (V2) no yes
A micro-USB cable that carries data no yes
A battery pack with 2 AAA batteries no only for projects you carry or wear

Every lesson, exercise, and project works in the simulator. A real board adds something the screen can't: the feel of shaking dice in your hand, wearing a badge, or walking around with a step counter. If your school or library lends micro:bits, borrow one for the motion and sound modules.

💡 Tip

If you get a board, get a V2. You can spot one by its gold logo and the small notches in the gold edge connector. The older V1 has no speaker, microphone, or touch logo, and programs that use those parts show the number 927 on its screen instead of running.

#Meet the board

Every invention you build follows the same shape: something in the world changes (an input), your code decides what that means, and the micro:bit does something you can see or hear (an output). Here is where each kind lives on the board.

A few of these hide in surprising places:

  • The light sensor is the LED screen itself. The same LEDs that light up can also measure how much light falls on them.
  • The temperature sensor is inside the main processor chip, so it reads the chip's temperature, which is usually close to the room's.
  • The microphone is a tiny hole on the front, with a small LED beside it that lights while the microphone is listening.
  • On the back you'll find the reset button, the USB socket, the battery socket, and a small light that flashes while a program is being copied onto the board.

#Open MakeCode and make a project

These steps are the same on every computer:

  1. Open your browser and go to makecode.microbit.org.
  2. On the home page, under My Projects, click New Project.
  3. Type a name such as c4t-hello and click Create.

The editor opens with two blocks already on the workspace: on start and forever. That's your proof the editor loaded. Which browser to use depends on your computer and whether you'll connect a real board:

Windows

Use Microsoft Edge (already installed) or Google Chrome. Both can send programs straight to a micro:bit over USB, so you'll never need to drag files around. Firefox also runs the editor and simulator, but it saves programs as files that you copy to the board yourself.

To make MakeCode easy to reopen, pin the tab or add it to your favorites. After the first visit the editor is cached, so it keeps working if the internet drops out.

macOS

Use Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge if you plan to connect a real board: they can send programs straight to it. Safari runs the editor and simulator perfectly well, but it can't talk to USB devices, so it downloads each program as a file that you drag onto the board in Finder. If you're simulator-only, any of the three is fine.

Chromebook

Use the built-in Chrome browser. It can send programs straight to a micro:bit over USB.

On a school-managed Chromebook, your administrator may have switched off direct USB access. If MakeCode later says WebUSB is disabled by browser policies, you can still download programs as files and copy them with the Files app; the next lesson shows how.

#A tour of the editor

Take a minute to find each of these, because every later lesson refers to them by name:

  • Simulator (left). A virtual micro:bit that runs your program and restarts every time you change the code. Click its A and B buttons with the mouse.
  • Toolbox (middle). Blocks grouped into colored categories: Basic, Input, Music, LED, Radio, Loops, Logic, Variables, Math, and more under Advanced. A search box sits at the top.
  • Workspace (right). Where you snap blocks together.
  • Blocks / JavaScript switch (top center). The same program shown as blocks or as text. There's a Python view as well.
  • Download button (bottom left), with a ... button beside it for download options, then the project name box and a save icon.
  • Undo, redo, and zoom buttons (bottom right).

#How programs appear in this course

Lessons show programs as MakeCode JavaScript in boxes like this one. It's the exact text MakeCode generates from blocks, so you can build it from blocks or paste it in.

To paste a program:

  1. Click JavaScript at the top of the editor.
  2. Select everything in the text area and delete it.
  3. Paste the program, then click Blocks.

You'll see a show icon block (from the Basic category) sitting inside on start. Any code that isn't inside an event or a loop belongs to on start, which runs once when the board powers up. On the simulator:

🧪 Try it yourself

Click the heart picture inside the show icon block and choose a different icon. The simulator restarts and shows your new choice. Then switch to JavaScript and find the name that changed, such as IconNames.Happy.

#Fixes for the problems beginners hit

  • The editor never finishes loading, or the page is blank. School and library networks sometimes block it. Try a different browser first. If it's still blank, ask whoever runs the network to allow makecode.microbit.org. Ad or script blockers can cause the same thing, so try with them switched off.
  • There's no simulator. On a narrow window or small screen, MakeCode can hide it. Make the window wider, or look for the button that shows the simulator again.
  • The simulator makes no sound. Browsers block sound until you interact with the page. Click once inside the simulator and sound starts working.
  • A block in a lesson isn't where you expect. MakeCode updates now and then, and categories shift slightly. Type the block's name, such as show icon, into the toolbox search box.
  • Your project is gone the next day. You were probably in a private or incognito window, which throws away its storage when you close it. Use a normal window. Lesson 3 of this module covers saving properly.

Key takeaways

  • The MakeCode simulator runs every program in this course, so a real micro:bit is optional.
  • Inputs (buttons, logo, sensors) feed your code; outputs (LEDs, speaker) show the result.
  • Chrome and Edge can send programs straight to a board; Safari and Firefox download a file instead.
  • Code shown in makecode boxes can be pasted into the JavaScript view and turned into blocks.

#Further reading

  • micro:bit features overview (opens in a new tab): the official guide to every part of the board, with short videos for each sensor.
  • MakeCode reference (opens in a new tab): every block, with its JavaScript name and a small example. Keep it open in a tab.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Build a program that uses on start, forever, and a button event.
  • Run it in the simulator and prove the behavior comes from your code.
  • Match each block to its line of MakeCode JavaScript.
  • Send the program to a real micro:bit, if you have one, and fix the transfer problems that trip up most beginners.

A tool you haven't seen working is a tool you can't trust yet. So the first job is small and visible: get a program running, change one detail, and watch the change appear. If that works in the simulator and on a board, everything after this is about ideas, not setup.

#The program

Here's the whole thing. It greets you once, then shows a beating heart forever, and plays a note whenever you press button A.

#Step 1: Build it

Start a new project named c4t-hello, then either paste the code into the JavaScript view or build it from blocks:

  1. From Basic, drag show string into on start and change the text to Hi!.
  2. From Basic, drag two show icon blocks into forever. Set the second one to the small heart.
  3. From Input, drag on button A pressed onto an empty part of the workspace.
  4. From Music, drag play tone Middle C for 1 beat until done into the button block.

Switch between Blocks and JavaScript a few times. The two views are the same program, and editing either one updates the other.

#Step 2: Run it in the simulator

The simulator starts by itself. Watch it and click its A button.

Three parts of the program are at work. on start runs once, which is why "Hi!" never comes back. forever runs its blocks, rests for a moment, and starts over, so the heart keeps beating. There's no pause block, yet each heart stays up for 0.6 seconds, because show icon holds its picture for 600 milliseconds before the next block runs. The button block is an event: it does nothing until A is pressed and released, then runs its note.

💡 Tip

No sound? Browsers stay silent until you interact with the page. Click once inside the simulator, then press A again.

🧪 Try it yourself

Prove the simulator is running your code. Change "Hi!" to your initials and watch the simulator restart with the new text. Then add a pause (ms) 1000 block from Basic at the end of forever and predict how the heartbeat changes before you look.

#Step 3: Read it as JavaScript

Each block became one line of text. Knowing the mapping lets you read any program in this course:

JavaScript Block Category
basic.showString("Hi!") show string "Hi!" (inside on start) Basic
basic.forever(function () { ... }) forever Basic
basic.showIcon(IconNames.Heart) show icon (heart) Basic
input.onButtonPressed(Button.A, function () { ... }) on button A pressed Input
music.play(music.tonePlayable(262, ...), ...) play tone Middle C for 1 beat until done Music

The 262 is Middle C written as a frequency: the speaker vibrates 262 times per second. In blocks you pick notes from a little piano instead.

#Step 4: Send it to a real micro:bit (optional)

If you have no board, skip to the quiz; the simulator has already proven your program works. With a board, there are two routes, and your browser decides which one you get.

Plug the micro:bit into the computer with the USB cable first. A drive called MICROBIT appears, the same way a USB stick would.

Windows

Chrome or Edge (direct):

  1. Click Download. MakeCode asks you to connect your micro:bit; click Next, then Pair.
  2. In the browser's device list, choose BBC micro:bit CMSIS-DAP (it may say DAPLink CMSIS-DAP) and click Connect.
  3. Click Download again if needed. From now on, one click on Download sends the program.

Firefox or any other browser (file):

  1. Click Download. A file whose name starts with microbit- lands in your Downloads folder.
  2. Open File Explorer and drag that file onto the MICROBIT drive, or right-click it and choose Send to, then MICROBIT.

macOS

Chrome or Edge (direct):

  1. Click Download. When MakeCode asks you to connect your micro:bit, click Next, then Pair.
  2. Choose BBC micro:bit CMSIS-DAP (or DAPLink CMSIS-DAP) in the list and click Connect.
  3. From now on, Download sends programs straight to the board.

Safari (file):

  1. Click Download. The .hex file goes to your Downloads folder.
  2. Open Finder, find MICROBIT under Locations, and drag the file onto it.
  3. macOS may warn that a disk wasn't ejected properly. That's expected: the micro:bit restarts itself to run the new program, which makes the drive vanish for a moment.

Chromebook

Chrome (direct):

  1. Click Download, then Next and Pair when MakeCode asks.
  2. Choose BBC micro:bit CMSIS-DAP (or DAPLink CMSIS-DAP) and click Connect.

If direct USB is blocked on a school device:

  1. Click the ... button next to Download and choose Download as File.
  2. Open the Files app, find the file in Downloads, and drag it onto MICROBIT in the left sidebar.

What success looks like: the small yellow light on the back flickers for a few seconds, the board restarts, "Hi!" scrolls by, and the heart starts beating. Press the real A button and the speaker on the back plays the note. If you look inside the MICROBIT drive afterward, the .hex file isn't there. That's normal: the board reads the file, stores the program, and throws the file away.

#Step 5: Run it without a computer

Unplug the USB cable. The program is stored in the board's memory, so it doesn't vanish. Connect the battery pack's white plug to the battery socket on the back (it only fits one way, so don't force it) and the heart starts beating again. Press the reset button on the back to restart the program from on start. On a V2, holding reset for about four seconds switches the board off; press it again to switch it back on.

#When the transfer doesn't work

  • No MICROBIT drive, or the board isn't in the pairing list. The usual culprit is a cable that only charges and carries no data. Try a different cable, then a different USB port.
  • "Failed to connect." Another tab, maybe a second MakeCode window or the micro:bit Python Editor, is already holding the connection. Close it, unplug the board, plug it back in, and try again. Download as File always works as a backup.
  • The board still runs the old program. You probably dragged an older file. Repeated downloads get names ending in (1), (2), and so on, so sort your Downloads folder by date and use the newest.
  • A sad face, then 927. The board is a V1 and the program uses a V2-only block. Playing sound through the built-in speaker is one of them, so this program shows 927 on a V1 when you press A.
  • An old V1 won't pair at all. It may need a firmware update. Open DETAILS.TXT on the MICROBIT drive; if the version number is below 0249, follow the firmware link in Further reading.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1There's no pause block in forever, yet each heart stays up for about 0.6 seconds. Why?

  • It only rests for a few milliseconds between passes, far less than 0.6 seconds.

  • That built-in hold is what sets the heartbeat speed.

  • The real board beats at the same speed.

Show answer

B. That built-in hold is what sets the heartbeat speed.

2You download with Safari, drag the file onto MICROBIT, and the board still shows yesterday's program. What's the most likely cause?

  • Safari can't use the direct route, but copying a downloaded file works fine.

  • The file always disappears after a successful copy; that's normal.

  • Repeated downloads stack up in your Downloads folder, so sort by date and use the newest.

Show answer

C. Repeated downloads stack up in your Downloads folder, so sort by date and use the newest.

  • Transfer code to the micro:bit (opens in a new tab): the official guide for every computer, plus tablets and phones.
  • WebUSB in MakeCode (opens in a new tab): the pairing steps with screenshots, and how to unpair a board.
  • Troubleshooting WebUSB (opens in a new tab): checking cables and firmware, and updating a V1 board.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain where MakeCode keeps your projects and back them up as files.
  • Name projects so you can find any version later.
  • Handle a micro:bit, a USB cable, and a battery pack safely.
  • Use zoom, themes, keyboard controls, and the text views to make the editor comfortable.
  • Follow a five-step routine when a program doesn't do what you expected.

Here's how students lose a week of work. They build a project on a shared school computer, the computer wipes its browsing data overnight, and the next morning My Projects is empty. Nothing was broken. MakeCode simply keeps your projects inside the browser you used, on the computer you used, and that storage can be cleared.

Ten minutes of habits now prevents that, along with the other two classic setbacks: a damaged board and a bug you can't find.

#Where your projects actually live

MakeCode saves your work automatically as you go, but "saved" means saved in the browser's own storage. Three things follow from that:

  • Another browser or computer can't see it. Projects made in Chrome don't show up in Edge, even on the same laptop.
  • Clearing browsing data deletes it. So does closing a private or incognito window.
  • "Untitled" projects pile up. Every project you never named is still there, which makes the one you want harder to find.

#Three ways to keep a project safe

  1. Download a copy. Click the save icon next to the project name box at the bottom of the editor. You get a .hex file that holds both the program the board runs and your blocks, so it works as a backup. To open it later, go to the MakeCode home page, click Import, then Import File..., and pick the file.
  2. Sign in. MakeCode works without an account, but you can sign in with a Microsoft, Google, or Clever account for free. Your projects then sync to the cloud and follow you to any computer.
  3. Share a link. The Share button makes a link to your project, which is handy for showing a teacher or asking for help.

⚠️ Watch out

A shared link is public: anyone who has it can open your project and read every block. Keep your full name, school, address, and phone number out of anything you share. For the name badge in the next module, use a first name or a nickname.

#Name projects so future-you can find them

Use one pattern for every project: the course, the module, what it is, and a version number when you try something risky.

Before a big change, download a copy of the working version first. If the change goes badly, import the copy and you're back where you were in seconds.

#Handle the hardware safely

A micro:bit is a bare circuit board with all its parts exposed on purpose, so you can see how it's built. That makes it easy to damage if you're careless. These rules come from the micro:bit Educational Foundation's safety guidance.

The board and the USB cable

  • Hold the board by its edges, and avoid touching the components while it's powered.
  • Before picking it up, touch something metal, like a table leg, to discharge static. Store it in its anti-static bag.
  • Power it only from a computer's USB port or the battery pack. Don't use phone power banks or charging ports marked with a lightning bolt or "SS"; they can damage the board.
  • Never lay metal objects (keys, coins, scissors) across the board. A short circuit can make it hot enough to burn.
  • Keep it away from water and wet hands, and don't leave it plugged in unattended.
  • Keep boards away from children under 8.

The battery pack

  • Use two AAA alkaline (or zinc) batteries. Don't use rechargeable batteries, and never try to recharge ordinary ones.
  • Don't mix old and new batteries, or different types, in the same pack.
  • Put the batteries in the right way round, and take dead ones out.
  • To unplug the pack, pinch the white plug and pull it out of the socket. Never pull on the wires.
  • If a board or battery pack ever feels hot, disconnect the power and tell an adult.

#Make the editor work for you

MakeCode has several settings for different needs. Try them now so you know they exist:

  • Zoom. Use the + and − buttons at the bottom right of the workspace for bigger blocks, or your browser's zoom (Ctrl and + on Windows and Chromebook, Cmd and + on a Mac) for everything.
  • Theme. The gear menu has a Theme option, including a high-contrast look.
  • Keyboard controls. The help menu (the question mark) has a Keyboard Controls page for building block programs without a mouse.
  • Text views. Prefer typing, or use a screen reader? The JavaScript and Python views are ordinary text editors, and every program in this course is shown as text.
  • Language. The gear menu also lets you change the editor's language.
  • On the board. If scrolling text is hard to read, slow it down: basic.showString("HELLO", 250) waits 250 ms between steps instead of the usual 150. Pairing a picture with a sound makes feedback easier to notice too.

#A routine for getting unstuck

When a program misbehaves, the urge is to change things at random until it works. That sometimes fixes the bug but rarely teaches you why. Work through these steps in order instead.

  1. Reproduce it in the simulator. If the simulator does the same wrong thing, the bug is in your code. If the simulator is fine but the board isn't, suspect the transfer, a V1 board running V2-only blocks, or a sensor that behaves differently in real life (the compass, for example, needs calibrating).
  2. Read what the screen shows. A sad face followed by a number is an error code, not a random glitch. 927 means a V2-only block on a V1 board; 020 means the board ran out of memory. The error codes page in Further reading lists the rest.
  3. Shrink the program. Drag suspicious blocks out of their event onto an empty part of the workspace. Loose blocks turn gray and stop running. Keep removing until the bug disappears; the last thing you removed is the suspect.
  4. Make hidden values visible. If you suspect a variable, show it with show number at the moment it matters. You'll practice this throughout the course.
  5. Explain it out loud. Walk through the program line by line to a friend, or to a rubber duck. You'll often hear your own mistake. If not, ask for help with a share link plus two sentences: what you expected, and what happened instead.
What you see Check this first
Pressing A does nothing Is the block on button A pressed, or did you pick B?
A picture flashes and is replaced instantly Is a forever loop drawing over it?
Works in the simulator, not on the board Did the download finish? Is the board a V2?
Sad face, then a number Look the number up in the error codes list

Check your understanding

2 questions

1You built a project on a library computer without signing in. Which habit protects it best?

  • The tab doesn't protect anything once the browser's storage is cleared.

  • The .hex file contains your blocks, and you can import it on any computer.

  • Naming helps you find it, but it still lives only in that browser.

Show answer

B. The .hex file contains your blocks, and you can import it on any computer.

2Your program runs fine in the simulator, but the real board shows a sad face and then 927. What's going on?

  • A numbered error code means the board is working and reporting a specific problem.

  • A charge-only cable would stop the program from arriving at all.

  • 927 is exactly that error; run it in the simulator or use a V2 board.

Show answer

C. 927 is exactly that error; run it in the simulator or use a V2 board.

  • Saving projects in MakeCode (opens in a new tab): how browser storage works and what clears it.
  • Error codes (opens in a new tab): what each number on a sad-face screen means.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Describe any micro:bit invention as an input, a decision, and an output.
  • Explain when on start, forever, and an event handler each run.
  • Choose between an event (on button pressed) and a check (button is pressed) for a task.
  • Predict when a picture appears if two parts of a program both want the screen.
  • Use the speaker as a second output, in the background or until done.

Maya's badge scrolls her name in a forever loop. She adds on button A pressed → show icon (happy) so visitors can tap it to say hi. A visitor presses A. Nothing happens. About three seconds later, after the visitor has walked off, the smiley appears for a moment and the name starts scrolling again.

Nothing in Maya's code is a typo; the program did exactly what it was told. Seeing why the smiley was late takes a clear picture of how the parts of a program take turns.

#Every invention is input, decision, output

An input is anything the micro:bit can notice. An output is anything it can do. Your code is the decision in between.

Invention Input Decision Output
Doorbell button A pressed always ring play a chime
Night light light level is it darker than 40? turn the LEDs on
Step counter accelerometer did that jolt look like a step? add 1 and show the count

Inputs come in two kinds: things that happen (a press, a shake, a clap) and things you measure (how bright, how tilted, how warm). The kind of input decides which kind of block you reach for.

#on start runs once, forever runs again and again

When the board powers up, on start runs from top to bottom, exactly once. Here that's the showString line, because code outside any block belongs to on start. Only when it finishes does forever begin. Forever runs its blocks, rests for 20 milliseconds, and runs them again, until the power goes off.

That short rest is when the board gives other parts of your program a turn, which is why a loop that never ends doesn't freeze the micro:bit. You can have several forever blocks; each takes its turns alongside the others.

🧪 Try it yourself

Predict how long one full heartbeat takes, then count it on the simulator. (show icon holds its picture for 600 ms by itself, so the answer is more than one second.)

#Events: code that waits for something to happen

An event handler sits idle until something happens, then runs. These three come from Input › on button pressed, with the dropdown set to A, B, and A+B. Press A in the simulator and an arrow points left, toward the A button. Because the program uses A+B, the simulator adds an A+B button.

Two details explain a lot of confusing behavior later:

  • "Pressed" means pushed down and released. The handler runs when you let go, not when you touch the button. For A+B, both buttons must be down, and the handler runs when you release one of them.
  • Handlers run alongside forever, not instead of it. A forever loop doesn't stop when you press a button. And if you press A again while the A handler is still running, the second press waits in line and runs when the first one finishes.

#Waiting for an event vs checking a button

Input › button A is pressed is a different kind of block. It doesn't wait for anything; it answers a yes-or-no question about this exact instant. That makes it right for "while you hold it" behavior:

Hold A and the center LED lights; let go and it goes dark. (led.plot lights one LED by its position; the next module uses it constantly.) This works because the loop asks about 50 times a second.

Now give that same loop something slow to do, like scrolling a word, and it only gets to ask the question between scrolls. A quick tap that starts and ends during a scroll is never seen. Step through a model of that loop below. Each entry in the list is one tenth of a second, and the button is tapped twice.

Both taps land while the loop is busy, so checking catches neither. An event catches both, because the board records each press and runs the handler as soon as it can. The rule of thumb:

You care about... Use Example
something that happened an event: on button pressed count presses, start a game
what's true right now a check: button is pressed inside forever a torch that's lit while held

#The screen does one thing at a time

Every show block (show string, show number, show icon, show leds, show arrow) takes over the whole screen and keeps it until it's done. show icon holds for 600 ms and show leds for 400 ms. Scrolling text moves one column every 150 ms, and each letter is about six columns wide, so "MAYA" keeps the screen busy for over three seconds.

If another part of the program asks for the screen while it's busy, that request waits its turn. That's the whole story of Maya's late smiley:

There are two ways to make a button feel instant. Keep the screen's jobs short, or cancel the current job before showing something urgent, using stop animation from LED › more:

led.stopAnimation() ends the scroll in progress, so the smiley appears the moment A is released. The forever loop then waits its turn and scrolls the name again after the smiley's 0.6 seconds. In the build-along you'll take this further, so a button press switches the badge to a new screen that stays.

#Sound is an output too

The play block in Music ends with a mode. until done makes the next block wait for the sound to finish; in background starts it and moves on, so here the tick appears while the melody plays. A V2 board plays it from the speaker on the back; the simulator uses your computer's speakers.

⚠️ Watch out

Timing adds up in ways you don't expect. A program that does basic.showIcon(IconNames.Heart) then basic.pause(1000) changes every 1.6 seconds, not every 1 second, because show icon already held for 0.6 seconds. When timing matters, count the hidden holds too.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1What does this program show? basic.showString("GO") at the top, then basic.forever(function () { basic.showIcon(IconNames.Heart) }).

  • On start always finishes before forever begins.

  • On start runs once; forever redraws the same heart each pass, so it looks steady.

  • "GO" is in on start, so it never runs again.

Show answer

B. On start runs once; forever redraws the same heart each pass, so it looks steady.

2You want a torch: the center LED is lit only while A is held down. Which approach fits?

  • That runs when A is released, and nothing turns the LED off again.

  • "While held" is about what's true right now, which is what a check answers.

  • This lights the LED for a fixed second after release, whatever you do with the button.

Show answer

B. "While held" is about what's true right now, which is what a check answers.

3Forever scrolls "SCORE". You press A, whose handler does basic.showIcon(IconNames.Yes), just as "SCORE" starts. When does the tick appear?

  • Only stop animation cuts a scroll short; this handler doesn't call it.

  • The show request waits for the busy screen, then forever takes the screen back.

  • The handler does get its turn; it just has to wait for the scroll.

Show answer

B. The show request waits for the busy screen, then forever takes the screen back.

4A forever loop checks button A is pressed, adds 1 to a counter, and then scrolls the counter. Fast taps are often lost. What's the best fix?

  • A slower loop checks less often and misses even more taps.

  • That shrinks the busy window but taps can still fall inside it.

  • The board remembers each press for you, so none fall between checks.

Show answer

C. The board remembers each press for you, so none fall between checks.

Key takeaways

  • On start runs once; forever repeats, resting 20 ms between passes so other code gets a turn.
  • Event handlers wait for something to happen and run alongside forever; "pressed" means pressed and released.
  • Use an event for things that happen and a check inside forever for things that are true right now.
  • Show blocks own the screen until they finish, and other show requests wait; stop animation cancels the current one.
  • play ... in background lets the program keep going while the sound plays.

m2-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Use a mode variable so a single forever loop owns the screen.
  • Make a button press take effect immediately with stop animation.
  • Change the LED brightness with set brightness.
  • Test a program against a written checklist in the simulator.
  • Wear the finished badge safely on battery power.

A badge has one job: tell a stranger something about you in the two seconds they spend looking at it. That means the screen has to change the moment you press a button, not when the current scroll happens to finish. In the notes you saw why the obvious version reacts late. Here you'll build one that doesn't.

#What we're building

The badge has three screens. Button A moves to the next one, and button B switches between bright and dim on any screen.

Use your own first name or a nickname in place of MAYA, and your own interest. Keep it to a first name: if you share the project link, everything in the code is public.

#Step 1: Scroll your name

Start a new project called c4t-m2-badge.

From Basic, drag show string into forever and type your name. The simulator scrolls it without stopping, because forever starts the scroll again as soon as the last one ends.

#Step 2: Add a mood button, the obvious way

Add on button A pressed from Input, with a show icon inside. Now test it like a visitor would: press A just as the first letter appears.

Two problems. The face is late, because the handler's show request waits for the scroll to finish. And it doesn't stay, because forever takes the screen straight back. Fixing the second problem first makes the first one easy.

#Step 3: Give the badge modes

The fix for "forever takes the screen back" is to stop having two parts of the program draw. Let forever be the only code that touches the screen, and have it draw whichever screen a variable says is current. The button just changes the variable.

To build it in blocks:

  1. In Variables, click Make a Variable... and name it mode. Put set mode to 0 in on start.
  2. From Logic, drag an if then else into forever. Click its + to add an else if.
  3. Use the = comparison from Logic for mode = 0 and mode = 1.
  4. In the A handler, use change mode by 1 from Variables, then an if that sets mode back to 0 when it's bigger than 2.

The numbers stand for screens: 0 is the name, 1 is the mood, 2 is the interest. The if (mode > 2) check makes the count wrap around from 2 back to 0 instead of climbing forever. Press A in the simulator and the screen changes, and this time it stays changed. But it's still late: the new screen only appears once the current scroll finishes.

#Step 4: React the instant A is pressed

Add stop animation from LED › more as the last block in the A handler. It cancels whatever the screen is in the middle of. The forever loop's current show block ends early, the loop finishes that pass, and about 20 ms later it starts a new pass, reads the new mode, and draws the right screen.

Notice that each branch of the forever loop has exactly one show block. That's deliberate. stop animation ends only the show block that's running right now, and the loop carries on with the rest of its pass. If the name branch showed a heart after the name, cancelling the name would let the heart play out for 0.6 seconds before the new screen appeared.

#Step 5: Dim and bright with button B

Both blocks live in LED › more. Brightness runs from 0 (off) to 255 (full). This handler doesn't need its own variable: it asks the screen how bright it is right now and flips to the other setting. A dimmer badge is easier on people's eyes indoors and lighter on the batteries.

#Step 6: Say hello with the logo (V2 only)

on logo pressed is in Input; the play sound block and the hello sound are in Music. As soon as you add it, the simulator switches to a V2 board with a gold logo you can click. The handler makes a sound but never touches the screen, so it can't interfere with the modes. If your board is a V1, skip this step: logo blocks show error 927 there.

#Step 7: Test against a checklist

Testing means deciding what should happen before you look. Run each row in the simulator and tick it off only if the result matches.

Test Expected result
Let it run for 10 seconds Your name scrolls again and again
Press A halfway through the name The happy face appears at once and stays
Press A again, then again The interest scrolls, then the name returns
From the name screen, press A five times fast The badge ends on the interest screen
Press B, then B again The screen dims, then goes back to full brightness
Click the logo A hello sound plays and the screen doesn't change

Why five presses land on the interest screen: 0 → 1 → 2 → 0 → 1 → 2. If it lands anywhere else, a press was lost or the wrap-around check is wrong.

#The finished program

#Step 8: Wear it safely

Download the program to your board, unplug the USB cable, and connect the battery pack. Then make it wearable:

  • Fasten the battery pack behind the board, with a case, a cardboard holder, or tape on the pack (not on the board's parts), so the wires never take the weight.
  • Make sure nothing metal touches the back of the board or the gold strip along the bottom: no lanyard clips, zips, keys, or coins. Metal across the pins can short-circuit the board.
  • If it feels warm, unplug the battery and check for anything touching the back.
  • When you're done for the day, unplug the pack by pinching the plug, not by pulling the wires.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does only the forever loop draw on the screen, while the buttons just change mode?

  • They are allowed; Step 2 did exactly that.

  • In Step 2, forever overwrote the handler's face. With one owner, the screen always matches mode.

  • Speed isn't the issue; the problem was two parts fighting over the screen.

Show answer

B. In Step 2, forever overwrote the handler's face. With one owner, the screen always matches mode.

2Suppose the name branch were basic.showString("MAYA") followed by basic.showIcon(IconNames.Heart). You press A halfway through the name. What do you see?

  • Stop animation only cancels the scroll; the heart block after it still runs.

  • The cancelled scroll returns early, the rest of the pass runs, and only the next pass reads the new mode.

  • The scroll really is cancelled; it's the block after it that gets in the way.

Show answer

B. The cancelled scroll returns early, the rest of the pass runs, and only the next pass reads the new mode.

3From the name screen, how many presses of A bring you back to the name screen?

  • Two presses take you to the interest screen (mode 2).

  • 0 → 1 → 2 → 0: the third press wraps back to the name.

  • The wrap happens on the third press, when mode would become 3.

Show answer

B. 0 → 1 → 2 → 0: the third press wraps back to the name.

Key takeaways

  • Let one forever loop own the screen and use a variable to choose what it draws.
  • Event handlers change the variable; stop animation makes the change show up immediately.
  • Keep one show block per branch, so cancelling it switches screens at once.
  • Write the test checklist before you run it, with the expected result for each action.
  • A wearable needs secured wires, no metal touching the back, and the battery unplugged when it's done.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a fourth screen, and make the wrap-around check use the new number.
  • Shake to show a random mood: an on shake event that sets mode to 1 and picks one of three icons.
  • Count visitors: each logo press adds 1 to a counter, and holding A and B together shows the total.
  • Return to the name screen automatically after 10 seconds on any other screen, using running time (ms) from Input.

#Further reading

  • Name tag project (opens in a new tab): MakeCode's step-by-step version, with variations on scrolling speed.
  • stop animation reference (opens in a new tab): what it cancels and a short example.
  • on logo event reference (opens in a new tab): the difference between pressed, touched, released, and long pressed.

m2-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Predict how long a sequence of show blocks and pauses really takes.
  • Pick between an event and a check for each button task.
  • Use a variable that a handler sets and a forever loop acts on.
  • Plan a multi-step input sequence as a set of states.

Every exercise runs in the simulator. Build it, predict what will happen, then run it. If the result surprises you, work out why before opening the solution; the surprise is where the learning is.

#Warm-up: how long is one pass?

How long does one pass take, and which face is on screen longer?

Show solution

One pass takes 1.6 seconds: 600 ms for the happy face, 600 ms for the sad face, plus the 400 ms pause. The sad face is on screen for 1 second, because it stays visible through the pause, while the happy face gets only 0.6 seconds.

#Exercise 1: A heartbeat at exactly 60 beats per minute

Make a heart that beats once per second: the big heart for half a second, then the small heart for half a second.

Need a hint?

In blocks, show icon always holds for 600 ms, which is too long. In JavaScript, basic.showIcon takes an optional second number: how many milliseconds to hold.

Show solution

The second argument replaces the 600 ms default, so each picture holds for 500 ms and a full beat takes one second. The show icon block has no slot for that number, so do this one in the JavaScript view. For an all-blocks version, draw each heart with show leds, which holds for 400 ms, and add pause (ms) 100 after each.

#Exercise 2: Arrows that point at the button

Pressing A shows an arrow pointing at the A button; pressing B shows one pointing at B. Either arrow disappears by itself after 2 seconds. Pressing both together shows a small diamond.

Need a hint?

show arrow is in Basic. A is on the left of the board, so its arrow points west. A handler can pause and then clear the screen.

Show solution

Each handler runs on its own, so pausing inside one doesn't freeze the others. Try pressing A, then quickly B: the right arrow replaces the left one, and the first handler's clear screen may blank it early. That's two handlers sharing one screen, the same problem the badge solved with modes.

#Exercise 3: A two-level torch

While A is held, light every LED at full brightness. While B is held, light them dim. When neither is held, the screen is dark.

Need a hint?

"While held" means you're checking what's true right now, so this belongs in forever with button A is pressed and button B is pressed from Input. set brightness is in LED › more.

Show solution

Events would be the wrong tool here: on button pressed runs only after you let go. You may notice the torch stays on for a moment after release. That's show leds holding its picture for 400 ms before the loop can check again.

#Exercise 4: A tap counter that never goes negative

A adds one and shows the count. B subtracts one and shows the count, but never goes below zero. A+B resets to zero.

Need a hint?

Make a variable count in Variables. Before subtracting, use an if to check that count is bigger than 0.

Show solution

let count = 0 sits outside every handler, so all three share the same variable and it keeps its value between presses. If you put let count = 0 inside the A handler, every press would start again from zero and the count would always show 1.

#Exercise 5: A doorbell that chimes

Pressing A shows a house and plays a two-note "ding-dong" (a high note, then a lower one), then clears the screen.

Need a hint?

Use play tone from Music twice with until done, so the second note waits for the first. 659 Hz is a high E and 523 Hz is a C.

Show solution

With in background, both notes would start almost together and the chime would sound like one note. Now press A twice quickly: the second ring waits until the first finishes, because a second press of the same button queues behind the running handler.

#Exercise 6: A crosswalk signal

The screen shows an X (don't walk). When someone presses B, wait 2 seconds, show a walking figure for 2 seconds, count down 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, then go back to the X. Pressing B again during the walk shouldn't add another walk afterward.

Need a hint?

Long sequences belong in forever, not in the handler. Let B set a variable requested to true; let forever check it, run the walk sequence, and set it back to false at the end.

Show solution

The handler just raises a flag and finishes instantly, so presses are never delayed. A press during the walk sets requested to true when it's already true, and the reset at the end clears it, so it's ignored. The countdown uses for index from 0 to 4 from Loops; 5 - index turns 0 to 4 into 5 down to 1. A single digit holds for about three quarters of a second, so with the pause each number lasts about a second.

#Challenge: A secret-knock lock

Make a lock that opens only after the sequence A, A, B. When it opens, show a tick and play a sound, then lock again. Any wrong press sends you back to the start, and shows an X for a moment.

Plan it as states before you write code. Each state answers one question: how much of the secret have I seen so far?

Need a hint?

One number variable, step, can hold the state: 0, 1, or 2. Each handler looks at step and decides where to go. Look closely at the arrow from "seen A A" on another A: why does it stay put instead of resetting?

Show solution

The A handler never resets: if you've pressed A, A, A, the last two presses are still A, A, so you're one B away from opening. B is the only press that can be "wrong", and it always sends you back to 0. Test it with A A B (opens), A B (X), and A A A B (opens).

m3-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Find any LED on the screen by its (x, y) coordinates and turn it on or off.
  • Explain why show blocks wipe out LEDs you plotted, and choose the right kind of block for a picture or a moving dot.
  • Use a variable to remember a position or a score, and keep it inside the screen's edges.
  • Pick random numbers with pick random.
  • Respond to the touch logo and the edge pins.

Type led.plot(5, 2) into a program and run it. Nothing lights up. There's no error message and no crash; the board simply ignores you. The screen has five columns, but they're numbered 0 to 4, so column 5 doesn't exist.

That one fact, counting from zero, explains most of the bugs people hit when they start drawing on the micro:bit. Once you have the coordinate system straight, the screen becomes a tiny game display you control one LED at a time.

#Every LED has an address

Each of the 25 LEDs has an address made of two numbers. x is the column, counting from the left edge. y is the row, counting from the top. Both run from 0 to 4, so the top-left LED is (0, 0) and the center is (2, 2).

Notice that y grows downward, the opposite of a math graph. Hold the board with the buttons on the left and right, the way it sits in the simulator, and (0, 0) is the top-left corner.

#Turn single LEDs on and off

These blocks live in the LED category. plot x y turns one LED on; unplot x y turns it off; toggle x y flips it. After the pause, the center LED goes dark because it was on and toggle flipped it. There's also point x y, a check that answers true if that LED is currently on. Under LED › more, plot x y brightness sets one LED to any brightness from 0 to 255.

🧪 Try it yourself

Change the program to light all four corners. Then add led.plot(5, 5) and confirm nothing new appears: anything outside 0 to 4 is silently ignored.

#Show blocks repaint the whole screen

The screen keeps a picture of all 25 LEDs in memory. plot and unplot change single dots in that picture. Every show block (show icon, show leds, show string, show number) replaces the entire picture at once. So order matters:

This shows the letter "d" and lights the top-left corner. Swap the two lines and the corner vanishes, because show string repaints all 25 LEDs and wipes your plot.

There's a second difference. Show blocks wait for the screen if it's busy and then hold their picture for a while. plot never waits and never holds: it changes the LED instantly. That makes plot the right tool for things that move, like a player in a game, and show blocks the right tool for whole pictures and messages. If you plot while a scroll is running, the next frame of the scroll paints over your dot.

For a picture you design yourself, use show leds from Basic and click the squares. In JavaScript it's a grid of # (on) and . (off):

#Variables remember where things are

A variable is a named box that holds a value your program can change later. To move a dot, you need to remember where it is. Make one in Variables › Make a Variable..., then use set to give it a value and change ... by to adjust it.

Each handler follows the same four moves: erase the dot where it is, change x, keep x on the screen, draw the dot where it is now. The two if blocks are a clamp: they stop x at the edges. Step through what happens to x when you press B three times and then A twice:

The third B tries to make x equal 5, and the clamp pulls it back to 4. Without the clamp, x would become 5, led.plot(5, 2) would do nothing, and the dot would seem to vanish off the edge.

#Random numbers keep things unpredictable

pick random 0 to 4 (in Math) gives a whole number from 0 to 4, and both ends are included. Games need it, or every round plays out identically.

Ten times a second this flips a random LED, which makes a twinkling screen. Change the range to randint(1, 6) and you have a dice roll, which you'll draw properly in the practice lesson.

#Two more inputs: the logo and the pins

The V2's gold logo is a touch sensor. on logo pressed in Input has a dropdown with four choices: pressed (touch and let go), touched (the moment your finger arrives), released (the moment it leaves), and long pressed. There's also logo is pressed, a check you can use in forever, just like button is pressed.

The three large gold pads on the edge, labelled 0, 1, and 2, work as touch inputs too. Hold the GND pad with one hand and touch pin 0 with the other, and on pin P0 pressed runs. In the simulator, just click the pad.

Single digits show without scrolling, which is why scores from 0 to 9 are easy to read in a game. From 10 upward, show number has to scroll.

⚠️ Watch out

A variable that never gets past 1. If you write let score = 0 inside a handler, a fresh score starting at zero is made on every press, so it always shows 1. Create the variable once, outside every handler (in blocks, put set score to 0 in on start), and only change it inside.

⚠️ Watch out

Swapped coordinates. led.plot(4, 1) is column 4, row 1: near the top right. If your drawing comes out flipped along the diagonal, you've given (row, column) instead of (x, y). The column always comes first.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1Which LED does led.plot(4, 0) light?

  • Bottom left is (0, 4): column 0, row 4.

  • x = 4 is the rightmost column and y = 0 is the top row.

  • Bottom right is (4, 4).

Show answer

B. x = 4 is the rightmost column and y = 0 is the top row.

2A program runs led.plot(0, 0) and then basic.showIcon(IconNames.Heart). Is the corner LED on afterward?

  • Show blocks repaint all 25 LEDs, so the plot is wiped.

  • The heart icon has that corner off, and show icon sets every LED.

  • Nothing fades; the heart simply overwrites it.

Show answer

B. The heart icon has that corner off, and show icon sets every LED.

3The moving-dot program has its two clamp if blocks removed. The dot starts at x = 2 and you press B three times. What do you see?

  • Nothing stops it any more; x goes to 5.

  • Out-of-range plots are ignored, not treated as errors.

  • x becomes 5, which plot ignores; one A press sets x to 4 and the dot reappears.

Show answer

C. x becomes 5, which plot ignores; one A press sets x to 4 and the dot reappears.

4Which values can randint(1, 6) return?

  • Both ends of the range are included.

  • pick random includes both the low and the high number.

  • The low end is 1, so 0 never appears.

Show answer

B. pick random includes both the low and the high number.

Key takeaways

  • x is the column from the left and y is the row from the top; both run from 0 to 4.
  • plot, unplot, and toggle change one LED instantly; show blocks repaint the whole screen and hold.
  • Plotting outside 0 to 4 does nothing, so clamp positions at the edges.
  • Create variables once, outside handlers, and change them inside.
  • The logo and the pins 0, 1, and 2 are extra touch inputs with their own events.

#Further reading

  • LED screen (opens in a new tab): the coordinate grid and the display buffer, with examples.
  • Variables in MakeCode (opens in a new tab): making, setting, and changing variables in blocks.
  • plot reference (opens in a new tab): plot, with a loop that draws a square border.

m3-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Organize a game as a set of states held in one variable.
  • Use pick random to make a wait that players can't predict.
  • Measure a time interval with running time (ms).
  • Spot and fix two fairness bugs: guessing the timing, and a "go" signal that isn't ready when it appears.
  • Keep a best score that survives between rounds.

Ask a friend to press a button "as soon as the screen lights up". If the screen always lights two seconds after they start, they'll stop watching and start counting, and their times will be impossibly fast. A reaction game is only fair if the player can't predict the signal, can't win by pressing early, and is timed from the exact moment the signal appears. Each of those becomes a step in this build.

#What we're building

The game moves between a few states. Each state has its own picture, so the player always knows what's going on, and each press of A means something different depending on the state.

State What the screen shows What pressing A does
idle an arrow pointing at A starts a round
waiting one dot in the center false start: shows an X
go every LED lit stops the clock and shows your time

#Step 1: A state variable and the idle screen

Start a project called c4t-m3-reaction.

Make a variable state in Variables and set it to the text "idle" in on start (use the text block from Text under Advanced, or just type the word in JavaScript). Then add show arrow pointing West, at the A button. Using words like "idle" instead of numbers costs nothing and makes every if you write later read like a sentence.

#Step 2: Start a round, then wait a random time

The button handler only starts the round: it sets the state, clears the screen, and plots a calm center dot. The waiting happens in forever, which checks the state, pauses for a random 1 to 4 seconds, and lights the whole screen.

Why put the pause in forever instead of in the A handler? Because of how presses queue. If the A handler were busy pausing, a second press of A during the wait would sit in line until the pause ended, then run instantly, and the player would get a "reaction time" of almost zero. Keeping the handler short means every press is handled the moment it happens.

The second if (state == "waiting") after the pause isn't a typo. A lot can happen in four seconds. In Step 4, an early press will change the state, and this check makes sure the screen doesn't light up for a round that's already over.

#Step 3: Measure the reaction

Input › running time (ms) tells you how many milliseconds have passed since the board started. Read it once when the signal appears and once when the player presses; the difference is the reaction time.

And in the A handler, a new branch:

The order of the three lines before show leds is the second fairness fix. show leds lights the screen and then holds for 400 ms before the next block runs. If state = "go" came after show leds, a quick player who pressed within those 400 ms would still find the state at "waiting" and be told they'd jumped the gun. Recording the time and switching the state first means the game is ready the instant the screen lights.

#Step 4: Catch false starts

A press during the wait ends the round with an X. Setting the state back to "idle" is what the second check in forever was for: when its pause ends, it sees the round is over and doesn't light the screen.

#Step 5: Remember the best time

In the go branch, after working out reaction, add:

best starts at 0, which here means "no rounds yet". The || (an or block from Logic) lets the first real time become the best automatically. B only works when the game is idle, so it can't clutter the screen during a round.

#The finished program

In blocks, every variable belongs to the whole program, so the finished version declares reaction at the top with the others. It's still only set in the go branch.

#Step 6: Test that it's fair

Test Expected result
Play five normal rounds Each wait feels different; times are a few hundred ms
Press A during the dot X, then the arrow; the screen never lights for that round
Press A the moment the screen lights A time is shown, never an X
Press B before playing 0 (no best yet)
Play three rounds, then press B The smallest of your three times

In the simulator your times include the mouse and the browser, so expect a few hundred milliseconds. On a real board with your thumb resting on the button, times usually come out a little faster and more consistent.

💡 Tip

on button pressed runs when you release the button, so every time includes how long your thumb stayed down. Tap, don't hold, and everyone's times stay comparable. For timing from the moment the button goes down, the on event block in Control (under Advanced) can listen for MICROBIT_BUTTON_EVT_DOWN from button A instead.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the game wait a random 1 to 4 seconds instead of exactly 2 seconds?

  • The wait length makes no difference to power use.

  • If the signal is predictable, the game measures counting, not reaction.

  • basic.pause(2000) would work fine; it would just be unfair.

Show answer

B. If the signal is predictable, the game measures counting, not reaction.

2What goes wrong if state = "go" is moved to after the show leds block?

  • Show leds holds for 400 ms before the next line runs.

  • During the hold the state is still "waiting", so a correct fast press counts as a false start.

  • The time is still measured from goTime; the problem is the wrong state.

Show answer

B. During the hold the state is still "waiting", so a correct fast press counts as a false start.

3Why is the random pause in forever instead of inside the A handler?

  • They can; pick random works anywhere.

  • Keeping the A handler short means each press is judged at the moment it happens.

  • The pause is equally accurate in either place.

Show answer

B. Keeping the A handler short means each press is judged at the moment it happens.

Key takeaways

  • Name your game's states and keep the current one in a single variable; each input then does one clear thing per state.
  • An unpredictable wait, a false-start rule, and an instant "go" state are what make a reaction game fair.
  • Time an interval by subtracting two readings of running time (ms).
  • Put long waits in forever and keep button handlers short, so presses are judged when they happen.
  • A best score can start at a value that means "none yet", like 0.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Two players. A and B both wait for the flash; the first press wins, and a press during the wait loses. (This is the practice lesson's challenge.)
  • Sound the start. Play a short tone at the flash and see whether times get faster with sound than with light.
  • Average of five. Add up five rounds and show the average, which is a fairer score than a single lucky round.
  • Hunt a sneaky bug. False-start and then press A again straight away: the forever loop is still in its old pause, so the new round's wait is whatever was left of it. Fix it with a round counter that forever checks after its pause.

#Further reading

  • Reaction time project (opens in a new tab): MakeCode's version, which uses pins and foil as the buttons.
  • running time reference (opens in a new tab): what the number means and how to time things with it.
  • show leds reference (opens in a new tab): drawing your own pictures, and the hold time after each one.

m3-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Use loops with plot and unplot to draw shapes and patterns.
  • Move a dot with clamping or wrap-around, using the remainder operator.
  • Keep scores in variables and combine numbers and text on the screen.
  • Turn a number into a picture, such as a dice face or a level bar.
  • Extend the reaction game's states to two players.

Build each one in the simulator. Before you run it, say out loud what you expect to see; then check. Several of these reuse patterns from the notes and the reaction game, so if you get stuck, look back at those first.

#Warm-up: which LEDs light up?

Show solution

A diagonal line from the bottom-left corner to the top-right corner. When index is 0 the LED is (0, 4), the bottom left; when index is 4 it's (4, 0), the top right. The 4 - index flips the direction, because y counts down from the top.

#Exercise 1: Draw the border with one loop

Light every LED on the outside edge of the screen and leave the middle nine dark. Use one for loop, not 16 separate plot blocks.

Need a hint?

for index from 0 to 4 (in Loops) gives you 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Each pass can plot one LED on each of the four sides.

Show solution

The top row is every (x, 0), the bottom row every (x, 4), and the side columns every (0, y) and (4, y). The corners get plotted twice, which is harmless: plotting an LED that's already on changes nothing.

#Exercise 2: A dot that wraps around

Change the moving dot from the notes so that it wraps instead of stopping. Moving right from x = 4 brings it to x = 0, and moving left from x = 0 brings it to x = 4.

Need a hint?

remainder of ... ÷ ... in Math gives what's left over after dividing. The remainder of anything divided by 5 is always 0 to 4. Be careful with going left: in JavaScript, the remainder of -1 ÷ 5 is -1, not 4.

Show solution

Going right, (4 + 1) % 5 is 0, so the dot wraps to the left edge. Going left, adding 4 has the same effect as subtracting 1 on a loop of five positions, but it never makes a negative number: (0 + 4) % 5 is 4.

#Exercise 3: A two-player scoreboard

A gives player 1 a point and B gives player 2 a point. After each point, scroll the score like 2-1. The first player to reach 5 wins: scroll A WINS or B WINS and reset both scores.

Need a hint?

join in Text (under Advanced) glues numbers and text into one string. In JavaScript, "" + p1 + "-" + p2 does the same thing.

Show solution

The empty string "" at the front is what MakeCode writes for a join block: it makes the expression text from the very first piece, so the numbers are stuck together with the dash instead of being added. Both scores reset together, so a new game always starts at 0-0.

#Exercise 4: A level meter

A raises a level from 0 up to 5 and B lowers it back to 0. Draw the level as full-width rows lit from the bottom: level 1 lights the bottom row, level 5 lights the whole screen.

Need a hint?

Let forever own the screen and redraw from level, like the badge did with mode. Visit every LED with a loop inside a loop. Row 4 is the bottom, so a row is lit when 4 - row is less than level.

Show solution

4 - row counts rows from the bottom: the bottom row is 0, the top row is 4. At level 2, rows with a count of 0 and 1 are lit. Because the loop plots and unplots, lowering the level erases the top row instead of leaving it lit.

#Exercise 5: Real dice faces

Pressing A rolls a number from 1 to 6 and draws it as dots, the way a real die looks, instead of as a digit.

Need a hint?

Look for dots that several faces share. Odd numbers have a center dot. Every face from 2 up has the top-left and bottom-right corners. Faces from 4 up add the other two corners. Only 6 has the middle of each side.

Show solution

Four separate if blocks, not one if ... else if chain, because a single face can need several groups of dots: a 5 uses the center and all four corners. clear screen first, or dots from the last roll would stay lit. Keep this program: in the next module you'll roll it by shaking.

#Exercise 6: Fill the screen in reading order

Light the LEDs one by one, left to right along the top row, then the next row, and so on down to the bottom right, 80 ms apart. Then turn them off in the same order, and repeat.

Need a hint?

Number the LEDs 0 to 24 in reading order, as in the chart below. For LED number i, the column is the remainder of i ÷ 5, and the row is i ÷ 5 rounded down (round in Math has a floor option).

Show solution

Take LED 13: 13 % 5 is 3 and 13 / 5 rounded down is 2, so it's (3, 2), the fourth LED of the middle row. Turning one counter into two coordinates like this is how a long list of things can be laid out on a grid.

#Challenge: A two-player reaction duel

Turn the reaction game into a duel. Press A and B together to start a round. After a random wait the whole screen lights, and the first player to press their button wins: show an arrow pointing at the winner's side. A press during the wait loses the round for whoever pressed it.

Need a hint?

Keep the same three states and the same forever loop as the build-along. Pressing A and B together doesn't also trigger the separate A and B handlers, so it's safe to use as the start button. Each of the A and B handlers needs a branch for "go" (you win) and one for "waiting" (you lose).

Show solution

The winner is whoever's handler sets the state back to "idle" first. The loser's press then finds the state is already idle and does nothing, so there's never a second, conflicting arrow. A false start points the arrow at the other player, because they win that round.

m4-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Read acceleration on the x, y, and z axes in milli-g and explain why a board at rest reads about 1023.
  • React to gestures such as shake, tilt, and screen down with event blocks.
  • Calibrate the compass and turn a heading in degrees into a direction.
  • Read light level, temperature, and (on a V2) sound level, and know each one's range and quirks.
  • Make a decision from a noisy reading without it flickering.

Lay a micro:bit flat on a desk, where it isn't moving at all, and ask its accelerometer how much force it feels. You'd expect zero. The answer is about 1023, pointing straight down through the board.

That's gravity. An accelerometer can't tell "sitting still on Earth" from "speeding upward at one g in a rocket", so it reports gravity as a steady pull. That pull is how the board knows which way is up.

#The accelerometer measures force on three axes

Readings come in milli-g (mg), thousandths of the pull of Earth's gravity, so about 1000 means "one g". The board measures along three directions at once:

  • x: left and right, across the screen.
  • y: forward and back, between the logo end and the pin end.
  • z: up and down, straight through the board.

Flat on a desk with the screen facing up, the board reads x = 0, y = 0, and z = -1023. Tilt it and gravity shifts from z into x or y. Input › acceleration (mg) reads one axis, or strength, which combines all three into a single size of force.

serial write value (in Serial, under Advanced) sends a labelled number to the computer ten times a second. Run it, click the Show data button that appears under the simulator, and move your pointer over the board to tilt it. You'll get a chart like this:

Flat, gravity sits entirely in z. Tilted 45 degrees to the right, it splits between x and z, about 720 each, because the total pull is still about 1023. Shaken, all three swing far past one g as your hand adds force on top of gravity. And every line is fuzzy: even a board at rest never reports exactly the same number twice.

#Gestures: the board recognizes common movements for you

Deciding "was that a shake?" from raw numbers is real work, so the micro:bit does it for you. Input › on shake is an event with a dropdown of gestures: shake, logo up, logo down, screen up, screen down, tilt left, tilt right, free fall, and high-force jolts of 3g, 6g, and 8g.

The shake gesture fires when the readings swing strongly back and forth several times in quick succession, which is exactly the shaken section of the chart. That makes dice almost a one-liner:

When a program uses shake, the simulator adds a SHAKE button to the board. Swap show number for the dice faces from the last practice lesson and you have real dice. For the tilt gestures, move your pointer to one side of the simulator board.

Gestures, like buttons, come as an event and as a check. is screen down gesture (input.isGesture(Gesture.ScreenDown)) answers whether the board is face down right now, which suits "while" behavior, such as blanking the screen while the board lies face down.

#The compass: which way the top edge points

Input › compass heading (°) gives a number from 0 to 359: the direction the board's top edge (the logo end) is pointing, measured clockwise from magnetic north. So 0 is north, 90 east, 180 south, and 270 west. Hold the board flat, screen up, with the top edge pointing where you want to measure.

North needs two ranges, heading < 45 and heading >= 315, because the scale wraps around: 350 degrees and 10 degrees are both nearly north. In the simulator a compass needle appears around the board; drag it around the logo to change the heading.

On a real board the compass must be calibrated first, because every board and room has slightly different magnetic surroundings. The first time a program reads the compass, the screen scrolls TILT TO FILL SCREEN. Tilt the board slowly in every direction until all 25 LEDs are lit; a smiley means you're done. The calibration lasts until you download a new program, and calibrate compass (input.calibrateCompass()) redoes it on purpose.

#Light and temperature: slow, steady measurements

light level reads from 0 (dark) to 255 (bright), using the LED screen itself as the sensor. The very first reading in a program is always 0 while the sensor switches on, so a program that reacts to darkness should ignore its first reading or wait a moment.

temperature (°C) reads the temperature of the processor chip, which is usually close to the air around it. A board that's been busy, or held in a warm hand, reads a degree or two high. Compare it with a real thermometer once and you can correct for the difference in code.

plot bar graph (in LED) turns a number into a bar: here, the brighter the room, the more LEDs light. In the simulator, drag the light-level control that appears on the board; temperature gets a thermometer slider in the same way.

#The microphone (V2 only): loudness, not words

The V2's microphone sits behind the small hole on the front, with an LED beside it that lights while it listens. sound level reads loudness from 0 (quiet) to 255 (loud). It can't record or recognize words, only how loud things are. There's also an event, on loud sound (input.onSound(DetectedSound.Loud, ...)), and set loud sound threshold to choose what counts as loud.

Clap near a V2 and a surprised face appears. The simulator switches to a V2 board and shows a sound-level slider so you can "clap" by dragging it.

#Noisy readings need a margin

Every sensor jitters. A night light that switches on below 40 flickers when the room sits around 40, because readings of 38, 41, 39, 42 cross the line again and again. The fix is a margin: switch on below 35, but off only above 45, and in between keep doing whatever you were doing. The build-along uses the same idea to make a step counter count each step exactly once.

⚠️ Watch out

The compass jumps around or points the wrong way. It hasn't been calibrated since the last download, or it's near metal or a magnet: laptops, phones, speakers, steel table frames. Recalibrate away from them, then hold the board flat. In the simulator the compass is always perfect, so this only shows up on real hardware.

⚠️ Watch out

927 on the screen as soon as the program starts. The program uses sound level or on loud sound and the board is a V1, which has no microphone. Use a V2, or test that part in the simulator.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A micro:bit lies flat and perfectly still, screen up. What does input.acceleration(Dimension.Z) read?

  • The accelerometer always feels gravity, even at rest.

  • Gravity pulls straight down through the board, about one g along z.

  • Flat, all of gravity is on z; x and y read near 0.

Show answer

B. Gravity pulls straight down through the board, about one g along z.

2You want the screen to go blank while the board lies face down and come back when it's turned over. Which fits best?

  • An event runs once when it happens; nothing would bring the picture back.

  • "While" is about what's true right now, so a check inside forever suits it.

  • Shaking has nothing to do with which way the board faces.

Show answer

B. "While" is about what's true right now, so a check inside forever suits it.

3The compass reads 300. Which way is the top edge pointing, using the four-direction program above?

  • North starts at 315 in that program; 300 is just short of it.

  • 300 is at least 225 and less than 315, so the program shows W.

  • East is around 90, on the other side of the circle.

Show answer

B. 300 is at least 225 and less than 315, so the program shows W.

4A night light turns on when input.lightLevel() < 40 and off otherwise. At dusk it flickers rapidly. What's the best fix?

  • Slower checks just make it flicker slowly.

  • The flicker moves to a different light level but doesn't go away.

  • The gap between the two values absorbs the jitter, so small wobbles don't switch it.

Show answer

C. The gap between the two values absorbs the jitter, so small wobbles don't switch it.

Key takeaways

  • The accelerometer reports force in milli-g on x, y, and z; at rest it reads gravity, about 1023 in total.
  • Gesture events (shake, tilt, screen down, free fall) do the pattern-spotting for you; is ... gesture checks the current pose.
  • Compass headings run from 0 to 359 clockwise from north, need calibration on a real board, and suffer near metal.
  • Light reads 0 to 255 (first reading 0), temperature reads the chip in °C, and the V2 microphone reads loudness 0 to 255.
  • Use two thresholds with a gap between them so jittery readings don't flip a decision back and forth.

#Further reading

  • acceleration reference (opens in a new tab): the axes, the units, and how strength is calculated.
  • compass heading reference (opens in a new tab): directions and degrees, and using the compass in the simulator.
  • micro:bit sensors (opens in a new tab): the Foundation's guide to each sensor, with beginner projects for every one.
