m4-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Look at a motion signal before writing code that counts it.
  • Explain why "count readings above a line" overcounts, and fix it with an armed flag and two thresholds.
  • Test a counting rule on data in Python before trusting it on the board.
  • Keep sensing in its own forever loop so the display can never make it miss a step.
  • Turn a compass heading into an arrow that points north from any direction.

The quickest step counter is one block: on shake → change steps by 1. Put it in your pocket, walk 20 steps, and it might say 9. Shake it in your hand for two seconds and it says 4. The shake gesture detects shaking, a fast back-and-forth swing, and walking isn't that. A real step counter has to look at the force itself and decide, reading by reading, what counts as one step.

That's the problem this build solves. You'll finish with a wearable gadget that has two modes: a step counter, and a compass arrow that always points north, the start of a navigation aid.

#What we're building

#Step 1: Look at the signal first

Before writing any counting code, look at what a step looks like to the accelerometer. Start a project called c4t-m4-step-counter:

strength combines all three axes into one size of force, so it doesn't matter which way the board is facing in your pocket. Download this, hold the board, walk across the room, and click Show data under the simulator (or Show data Device when the board is connected by WebUSB). Each step makes a spike. Here's a model of 10 steps, shaped like a real recording:

Two things stand out. Each step is a spike well above the resting value of about 1000. And the line is fuzzy: even the tops of the spikes wobble up and down.

#Step 2: The obvious rule, and why it fails

The obvious rule is "add a step whenever strength is over 1400". Before putting it on the board, test it on the data, along with a slightly smarter version that only counts the moment the line crosses 1400 going up:

Counting readings is hopeless: each spike stays above the line for several readings in a row, so one step counts three or four times. Counting crossings is much closer, but still wrong. When the top of a spike wobbles across 1400 (above, a hair below, above again), that one step crosses twice.

#Step 3: Count once, then wait to be ready again

The fix uses two lines instead of one, and a variable called armed that remembers whether the counter is ready for the next step:

  • When armed is true and strength goes above 1400, count a step and set armed to false.
  • Only when strength falls below 1100 does armed become true again.

Wobbles at the top of a spike can cross 1400 as often as they like; the counter isn't armed, so they're ignored. The gap between 1100 and 1400 is the same margin the night light used in the notes. Step through the rule on twelve readings:

The first spike dips to 1380 and climbs to 1530 again, which a single-line counter would count twice. Here it counts once, because armed stays false until the reading of 1050. Now test the rule on the full walk:

Ten for ten. Testing on data first meant you found and fixed the double-counting without walking a single step.

#Step 4: Put the sensing loop on the board

This is the same rule, line for line. The and block comes from Logic, and true and false are the true and false blocks from Logic too. There's no pause: forever already rests 20 ms between passes, so it takes about 50 readings a second, the same rate as the data above. And there's no show block. That's deliberate.

#Step 5: A separate display loop

Add a second forever block for the display. Showing a two-digit count scrolls for over a second. If that scroll lived in the sensing loop, every step you took during it would be missed: the busy-loop problem from the buttons module, now with footsteps. With two loops, the sensing loop keeps reading while the display loop scrolls.

To test in the simulator, you need to push the strength above 1400. Over most of the simulator board it stays at 1023, however you tilt it. Move the pointer right into a corner of the board, where the simulated force rises well above 1400, then back to the middle. Each trip should add exactly one step. On a real board, walk 20 steps and compare. If it undercounts, try 1300; if it counts while you stand still, try 1500.

#Step 6: An arrow that always points north

compass heading tells you which way the board's top edge points. To point at north, turn that around. If the top edge faces east (90), north is 90 degrees to your left. In general, north is (360 - heading) % 360 degrees clockwise from the top edge.

The micro:bit has eight arrows, numbered 0 to 7 clockwise from straight up: North, North East, East, South East, South, South West, West, North West. Divide the angle by 45 and round to get the nearest arrow:

Top edge faces heading 360 - heading arrow number arrow shown
north 0 0 0 up
east 90 270 6 left
south 180 180 4 down
north-west 315 45 1 up and right

Add the compass branch to the display loop:

The final % 8 handles one edge case: an angle like 350 rounds to arrow 8, which doesn't exist, and 8 % 8 turns it back into 0, straight up. In the simulator, drag the compass needle around the logo and watch the arrow swing the opposite way, always toward north. On a real board, the first time compass mode runs, the screen asks you to TILT TO FILL SCREEN; finish the calibration before trusting the arrow.

#Step 7: Buttons to switch modes and reset

Same pattern as the badge: handlers change a variable, stop animation makes the change show at once, and only the display loop draws.

#The finished program

Test it like the badge: in steps mode, three corner trips should give 3; B should switch to an arrow; dragging the needle should move the arrow; A+B should bring the count back to 0. For a walk, clip the battery pack and board together so the wires can't snag, and keep the board away from keys and coins in your pocket.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why are sensing and display in two separate forever loops?

  • A loop can hold as many show blocks as you like.

  • While one loop scrolls a number, the other keeps reading about 50 times a second.

  • The sensing loop reads at the same rate either way; the point is that nothing interrupts it.

Show answer

B. While one loop scrolls a number, the other keeps reading about 50 times a second.

2You remove the else if (strength < 1100) part and instead set armed = true whenever strength is below 1400. What happens?

  • With one line, a wobble just below 1400 re-arms the counter mid-step.

  • That's the single-line crossing counter from Step 2, which counted 12 instead of 10.

  • It still counts; it just counts some steps twice.

Show answer

B. That's the single-line crossing counter from Step 2, which counted 12 instead of 10.

3You face south, so the heading is 180. Which arrow does compass mode show?

  • Up would mean north is straight ahead, but you're facing away from it.

  • (360 - 180) % 360 is 180, arrow 4, which points down: north is behind you.

  • Left is for facing east, when north is on your left.

Show answer

B. (360 - 180) % 360 is 180, arrow 4, which points down: north is behind you.

Key takeaways

  • Plot a sensor's signal before writing code that interprets it.
  • Two thresholds and an armed flag count each spike once, even when its top wobbles.
  • Test a counting rule on recorded or modelled data before trusting it on the board.
  • Put sensing and display in separate forever loops so slow drawing can't cause missed readings.
  • To point at north, use (360 - heading) % 360 and divide by 45 to pick one of the eight arrows.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Show progress toward a goal with led.plotBarGraph(steps, 100) instead of the number.
  • Estimate distance: measure your stride once, then show steps times your stride length in meters.
  • Add a third mode that shows N, E, S, or W as a letter, using the four-direction program from the notes.
  • Play a short sound every 100 steps, using in background so it never delays the display.

#Further reading

  • Step counter project (opens in a new tab): the Foundation's beginner version, which uses the shake gesture; compare it with yours.
  • calibrate compass reference (opens in a new tab): when calibration runs and when it has to be repeated.
  • plot bar graph reference (opens in a new tab): turning a number into a bar, for the progress-goal extension.

m4-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Combine gesture events with drawing code from earlier modules.
  • Use two thresholds to make a sensor decision that doesn't flicker.
  • Convert a sensor range into screen coordinates, and keep the result on the screen.
  • Count sound events and avoid the board hearing itself.
  • Pick from a list of labels with an array index, and smooth a noisy reading.

Each of these runs in the simulator, which adds a control for every sensor you use: a SHAKE button, a light-level dial, a thermometer slider, a compass needle, or a sound-level slider. A real board makes the motion and sound exercises more fun, but it's never required.

#Warm-up: what pose is the board in?

Match each set of readings to a pose: flat with the screen up, flat with the screen down, or falling.

Show solution

(a) is flat with the screen up: all of gravity is along z, pointing down through the back. (b) is flat with the screen down: same size, opposite sign, because the board is upside down. (c) is falling. In free fall everything drops together, so the accelerometer feels almost no force; that's how the free fall gesture works.

#Exercise 1: Shake dice with real faces

Shaking the board rolls a number from 1 to 6, draws it as dice dots (the faces from the last practice lesson), and plays a short sound.

Need a hint?

Start from your dice-faces solution and swap on button A pressed for on shake in Input. Put the sound in background so the face appears at once.

Show solution

Only the event changed: the drawing code doesn't care why it was asked to roll. Click SHAKE in the simulator a few times and check that you see all six faces eventually.

#Exercise 2: A night light that doesn't flicker

Light the whole screen when the room gets dark and switch it off when it's bright again. Use a margin so it doesn't flicker at dusk: on below 35, off above 45.

Need a hint?

You need a variable lit that remembers whether the light is on, because between 35 and 45 the answer is "keep doing what you were doing". Remember that the very first light reading is 0, so wait a moment before the first check.

Show solution

Between 35 and 45 neither branch runs, so the light stays as it was. The half-second pause in on start skips past the switch-on reading of 0, which would otherwise light the screen for an instant every time the board starts. Drag the simulator's light control slowly through 35 to 45 in both directions to test the margin.

#Exercise 3: A thermometer with a heat warning

A shows the temperature in °C, B shows it in °F, rounded to a whole number. If the temperature reaches 30 °C, play a warning sound once. Don't warn again until it has dropped below 28 °C.

Need a hint?

°F = °C × 1.8 + 32. round is in Math. The "warn once" rule is the night-light margin again, with a variable warned.

Show solution

Temperature changes slowly, so checking once a second is plenty. Without warned, the alarm would replay every second for as long as the room stayed hot.

#Exercise 4: A spirit level

Show a single dot that rolls toward the low side of the board, like the bubble's opposite in a spirit level. Flat, the dot sits in the center. Tilted fully right, it's on the right edge; tilted toward you, it slides to the bottom.

Need a hint?

x and y run from about -1023 to 1023 when you tilt. Adding 1023 gives 0 to 2046, and dividing by 512 and rounding gives 0 to 4. Shaking can push readings past 1023, so keep the result between 0 and 4 with min and max from Math. If the dot runs uphill on your board, put a minus sign in front of that reading.

Show solution

Flat, x is 0, so (0 + 1023) / 512 is just under 2 and rounds to 2: the center column. At x = 1023 it rounds to 4. Math.max(col, 0) lifts anything below 0 up to 0, and Math.min(..., 4) caps anything above 4. In the simulator, move your pointer around the board and watch the dot follow.

#Exercise 5: A clap counter (V2)

Count claps. Each loud sound adds one and shows the total; A+B resets it. Then make it beep on every clap and find out what goes wrong.

Need a hint?

on loud sound and set loud sound threshold are in Input. Try a threshold around 150 and adjust. For the beep: where does the speaker's sound go?

Show solution

Add a beep inside the sound handler and, on a real board, the count may start climbing by itself: the microphone hears the board's own speaker, which counts as another loud sound, which beeps again. Fix it by keeping the beep quiet with set volume in Music, or by not beeping at all. Talking loudly near the board can also add claps, so tune the threshold in a quiet room.

#Exercise 6: An eight-point compass

Show the direction the top edge faces as one of eight labels: N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW.

Need a hint?

Each label covers 45 degrees. Math.round(heading / 45) % 8 turns a heading into a number from 0 to 7. An array from Arrays (under Advanced) can hold the eight labels in order, and get value at picks one by its index.

Show solution

A heading of 100 gives 100 / 45, about 2.2, which rounds to 2: "E". A heading of 350 rounds to 8, and % 8 wraps it to 0: "N". The array replaces a chain of seven else if blocks, and putting the labels in the same order as the arrows makes the index do all the work.

#Challenge: A steady light meter

led.plotBarGraph(input.lightLevel(), 255) jitters even when the room isn't changing. Smooth it: keep a variable smooth and, on every pass, move it one fifth of the way toward the new reading. Show smooth as the bar graph. Then turn a lamp on and off and describe the trade-off.

Need a hint?

"Move one fifth of the way" is smooth = smooth + (light - smooth) / 5. Start smooth at a first real reading, not at 0, or the bar will creep up from nothing every time the board starts.

Show solution

Each pass closes a fifth of the gap between smooth and the newest reading, so a single odd reading only nudges the bar. The cost is lag: after a real change, the bar takes several passes to catch up, as the chart shows. Divide by 2 for a quicker but jumpier bar, or by 10 for a steadier but slower one. Choosing that number is a design decision, and the right answer depends on whether your invention cares more about speed or steadiness.

m5-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain why every micro:bit in range and in the same group hears a radio message.
  • Choose a group with radio.setGroup so your devices ignore everyone else's.
  • Send and receive numbers, strings, and name–value pairs, and match each sender to the right receive block.
  • Read one radio program in Blocks, JavaScript, and MicroPython, and name what changes between them.

Thirty students in one room press button A at the same moment. Every micro:bit in the room flashes a heart, including the ones that were supposed to stay dark. Nobody wrote a bug in the usual sense. They all left their radios on the same default group, so every board heard every other board.

That scene holds the core idea: messages go to everyone listening, and a group number you pick decides who is listening.

#A radio message is a shout, not a phone call

A phone call connects two people. A micro:bit radio message is more like shouting across a playground: anyone close enough who is paying attention hears it. The board's 2.4 GHz radio (the band Wi-Fi and Bluetooth use) broadcasts each message as one short packet. Three facts follow:

  • No address. You can't send to "Maya's badge". Every board in range and in your group gets the packet.
  • No receipt. The sender never learns whether anyone heard. If you need to know, the receiver has to send a reply, which you'll build in the next lesson.
  • Short range, short packets. Think "same room or the next one", carrying a number, a short text, or a label plus a number.

#Groups keep your conversation private

radio.setGroup(id) tunes your board to a group from 0 to 255. If you never call it, the board uses group 0, which is why the classroom above went wrong. Put setGroup in on start so it runs before any message goes out, and agree on the number with your partner.

Paste this into the JavaScript view at makecode.microbit.org. As soon as a radio block is in the project, the simulator draws a second micro:bit under the first. Press A on the top board and the bottom board scrolls HI.

Both simulated boards run the same program, so they always share a group. MakeCode's reference notes that setGroup only takes effect on real hardware, which is where groups matter: real badge pairs on groups 42 and 43 can sit side by side without hearing each other.

📝 Note

A group is a filter, not a lock. Anyone who sets their board to 42 hears your messages. Never send anything over micro:bit radio that you'd mind the whole room reading.

Here is the filtering rule as a tiny Python model: each board compares the packet's group with its own, then keeps or drops the message.

#Three kinds of message, three matching receivers

MakeCode can send three kinds of packet. Each one has its own receive block, and a board only reacts if it has the receive block that matches what was sent.

Send block Receive block What it carries Size limit
radio.sendNumber(n) radio.onReceivedNumber one number none worth worrying about
radio.sendString(s) radio.onReceivedString text 19 characters
radio.sendValue(name, n) radio.onReceivedValue a label and a number label up to 8 characters

sendValue is the one you'll use most for sensors, because the label says what the number means. A board that sends both temperature and light can label each reading, and the receiver sorts them out:

Drag the top board's temperature slider in the simulator and the bottom board's number follows. The if on name is the line that matters: without it, light readings would be shown as temperatures.

#One receive block per kind, with the decisions inside

A project can have only one onReceivedString block (and one each for numbers and values). To react to several different strings, make the decisions inside that one block:

Inside a receive block, radio.receivedPacket(RadioPacketProperty.SignalStrength) tells you how strong the signal was: about -128 when barely heard, up to about -28 on a V2 board right beside you.

#The same program in Blocks, JavaScript, and MicroPython

Blocks and JavaScript are two views of one MakeCode project. The switch at the top of the editor flips between them and translates your code both ways, so a Blocks badge and a JavaScript badge download the same program and talk perfectly. (The switch also offers a Python view; that's still the same MakeCode project, spelled in Python.)

MicroPython is a different system. At python.microbit.org you write real Python and the micro:bit runs a small Python interpreter. Here's the HI program in MicroPython. It runs on a micro:bit or in that editor's simulator; desktop Python stops at line 1 with an import error, because the microbit module only exists on the device.

Five differences stand out:

  1. Events versus a loop. MakeCode uses event blocks ("when A is pressed…"). MicroPython has no radio event, so the program loops and checks: was A pressed since last time? Is a message waiting?
  2. Asking for messages. radio.receive() takes the next message from a small waiting line (three by default) or returns None. Stop calling it and new messages are dropped.
  3. Setting the group. radio.config(group=42) instead of radio.setGroup(42).
  4. Only text. MicroPython's radio.send takes a string. To send a number, send str(n) and turn it back with int(message) on the other side.
  5. Indentation instead of braces. The lines inside if and while are indented; there are no { }.

One difference is invisible: MakeCode wraps each message in its own packet format, which MicroPython's radio.receive() doesn't understand. A MakeCode badge and a MicroPython badge won't read each other's messages without extra work, so keep all the boards in a project on one system.

#Mistakes that make radio go silent

⚠️ Watch out

Groups don't match. One board calls radio.setGroup(12), the other radio.setGroup(21), and messages vanish with no error. Fix: show the group on start with basic.showNumber(12) so you can compare boards at a glance.

⚠️ Watch out

Sender and receiver use different kinds. The sender calls radio.sendString("5") but the receiver only has onReceivedNumber. A string packet never triggers a number block. Fix: pick one kind and use the matching pair.

⚠️ Watch out

Text cut short. radio.sendString("Meet at the gym after lunch") arrives as Meet at the gym aft, because strings stop at 19 characters. sendValue labels stop at 8, so "temperature" arrives as temperat and never matches a check for the full word. Fix: short labels like "temp".

Check your understanding

4 questions

1Board A is on group 5 and sends radio.sendString("GO"). Board B is on group 5 and board C never calls setGroup. Both have an onReceivedString block. What happens?

  • C is on the default group 0, so it drops packets from group 5.

  • B shares group 5 with A. C sits on group 0 and never sees the packet.

  • Radio messages have no receiver address; everyone in the group gets them.

Show answer

B. B shares group 5 with A. C sits on group 0 and never sees the packet.

2The sender runs radio.sendValue("brightness", 60) and the receiver checks if (name == "brightness"). What does the receiver do?

  • It would if the label fit, but brightness has 10 characters and labels stop at 8.

  • The packet does arrive and the receive block runs, but the shortened name never equals "brightness".

  • MakeCode never crashes over a long label; it shortens it without telling you.

Show answer

B. The packet does arrive and the receive block runs, but the shortened name never equals "brightness".

3Why does the MicroPython version call radio.receive() on every pass of the loop?

  • radio.on() does that, once, before the loop.

  • Messages wait in a small queue until your code takes them out with radio.receive().

  • Receiving never sends anything; only radio.send does.

Show answer

B. Messages wait in a small queue until your code takes them out with radio.receive().

4One badge is coded in MakeCode Blocks and the other in MakeCode JavaScript, both on group 7. Can they talk?

  • They're two views of one project, so the downloaded code and its packet format are identical.

  • The view only changes how you see the code, not what runs on the board.

  • Any matching send and receive pair works, whichever view you wrote it in.

Show answer

A. They're two views of one project, so the downloaded code and its packet format are identical.

Key takeaways

  • A radio message is a broadcast: every board in range on the same group hears it, and the sender gets no receipt.
  • radio.setGroup (0–255) goes in on start; boards that skip it share group 0 with everyone else.
  • Match the pairs: sendNumber/onReceivedNumber, sendString/onReceivedString, sendValue/onReceivedValue. Strings stop at 19 characters, value labels at 8.
  • Use one receive block per kind and decide inside it with if.
  • Blocks and JavaScript are one MakeCode program; MicroPython loops and checks instead of using events, and its radio messages aren't compatible with MakeCode's.

#Further reading

  • MakeCode radio reference (opens in a new tab): every radio block with a working example, including signal strength and serial numbers.
  • micro:bit radio and pins (opens in a new tab): the Micro:bit Educational Foundation's plain-language guide to what the radio can do.
  • MicroPython radio tutorial (opens in a new tab): the same ideas from the MicroPython side, ending with a firefly program you can try in the Python editor.

What you'll learn

  • Build a two-board messenger in MakeCode that sends a labelled value by radio.
  • Add a receipt so the sender knows the message arrived, and a timeout for when it didn't.
  • Test both badges at once in the MakeCode simulator.
  • Port the program to MicroPython and explain each change you had to make.

Here's the finished messenger in action. Each badge holds a mood. Button A flips through four faces on your own badge, and button B sends the current face to your partner. Your partner's badge shows the face and beeps, then quietly sends back a receipt. If a receipt arrives within a second, you see a tick. If it doesn't, you see a cross, so you know to try again.

Open makecode.microbit.org, start a New Project, and switch to JavaScript with the switch at the top. You can flip back to Blocks at any step to see the same code as blocks.

#Step 1: Pick a group and show it

Agree on a group number with your partner first. This build uses 7. Showing the number at start-up is a cheap way to catch the most common radio bug: two badges quietly set to different groups.

The simulator now shows two micro:bits, and both scroll 7. That's your first proof that the second board is running the same program.

#Step 2: Choose a mood with button A

The mood is a number from 0 to 3, and a function turns that number into a face. Keeping the drawing in one function means every part of the program shows moods the same way.

Press A on the top board four times. You should see sad, surprised, asleep, then happy again. The % 4 wraps 3 back round to 0, so mood can never reach a number showMood doesn't know.

#Step 3: Send the mood with button B

sendValue sends a label and a number together. The label "mood" lets the receiver tell this message apart from anything else you add later.

The arrow is the sender's "it left my badge" signal. It does not mean anyone heard it; remember the radio never tells you that.

#Step 4: Receive the mood and show it

Add the matching receive block. It checks the label before trusting the number.

Test it: press A twice on the top board, then B. The top board shows an arrow and the bottom board shows the surprised face and beeps (if your browser plays simulator sound). Now try it the other way round. Both boards can send and receive, because both run every block.

#Step 5: Send a receipt back

To know the message arrived, the receiver has to say so. Add one line to the receive block so it answers with the string "GOT", and a string receiver that shows a tick when that answer comes back.

Press B on the top board again. The arrow should flick to a tick almost at once. Notice that the receipt is just another broadcast: in a room full of badges on group 7, everyone would see it. That's fine for a pair, and it's a problem you'll solve properly in the capstone.

#Step 6: Say so when no receipt arrives

A tick when things work is only half the job. If your partner is out of range, the sender should show a cross instead of an arrow that stays up forever. Two new variables remember whether we're waiting and when we sent. A forever loop checks the clock.

control.millis() is the number of milliseconds since the board started. Subtracting sentAt gives how long we've been waiting. Why not basic.pause(1000) after sending? Because a pause tells you nothing: you'd still have to find out whether "GOT" arrived during it. The waiting flag records exactly that.

To test the failure path in the simulator, you need the other board to stay silent. The easy way is to cheat for a moment: comment out radio.sendString("GOT") with //, press B, and watch the cross appear after a second. Put the line back when you're done.

#The finished program

If you have two real micro:bits, click Download and copy the same program to both. Hand one to a friend and walk apart until the ticks turn into crosses: that's your real range.

#Port it to MicroPython

Now open python.microbit.org in a new tab and rebuild the same badge in MicroPython. Paste this in, then run it in the editor's simulator. MicroPython code can't run as ordinary Python on your laptop; it stops with an error at from microbit import * because that module lives on the micro:bit.

The Python editor's simulator shows only one micro:bit, so you play the partner yourself. Open the Radio panel under the simulator and type mood:2 into the message box: the face should change. Press B on the simulated board and type GOT within a second to get a tick; wait longer and you'll get the cross.

Here's what changed, and why:

MakeCode MicroPython Why it changed
Five event blocks One while True loop MicroPython has no radio event, so the loop checks buttons and messages on every pass
radio.sendValue("mood", 2) radio.send("mood:2") MicroPython sends text only, so the label and number share one string
value arrives as a number int(message[5:]) Slice off the five characters mood:, then turn the rest into a number
showMood with an if chain MOODS[mood] Python lists can hold images, so one lookup replaces the chain
control.millis() running_time() Same idea, different name
radio.setGroup(7) radio.config(group=7) MicroPython sets every radio option through config

button_a.was_pressed() deserves a note. It answers "has A been pressed since I last asked?", so a quick tap during display.scroll still counts on the next pass. That's how a loop-based program avoids missing presses.

Remember that these two versions can't talk to each other. A MakeCode badge doesn't understand MicroPython's packets, and the other way round, so both badges in a pair need the same version.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the receiver send "GOT" back instead of the sender just assuming the mood arrived?

  • A sendValue packet is broadcast whether or not anyone answers.

  • Broadcasts have no receipt built in. The "GOT" string is a receipt you designed yourself.

  • The group is set once by radio.setGroup; replies don't change it.

Show answer

B. Broadcasts have no receipt built in. The "GOT" string is a receipt you designed yourself.

2The timeout check lives in a forever loop instead of basic.pause(1000) after sending. What does that buy you?

  • The flag records whether "GOT" arrived; the loop just compares the clock against sentAt.

  • The radio's speed doesn't change; only how the sender keeps track of time.

  • Nothing here blocks button A, and freezing buttons is the opposite of the goal.

Show answer

A. The flag records whether "GOT" arrived; the loop just compares the clock against sentAt.

3In the MicroPython version, why is the message "mood:2" and not just "2"?

  • It can send any text, digits included.

  • With only one radio.receive(), every kind of message arrives in the same place, so the text must say what it is.

  • There's no minimum length.

Show answer

B. With only one radio.receive(), every kind of message arrives in the same place, so the text must say what it is.

Key takeaways

  • Show the radio group on start-up; it turns the most common silent bug into something you can see.
  • Label your messages (sendValue in MakeCode, a prefix like mood: in MicroPython) so one board can handle several kinds.
  • A receipt plus a timeout turns "I sent it" into "they got it" or "they didn't", which is the difference between a toy and a tool.
  • Porting to MicroPython means replacing events with a loop that checks, packing numbers into text, and using Python's own names.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add more moods (there are dozens of IconNames), and keep the % 4 in step with the count.
  • Show how far away your partner is: in the receive block, plot radio.receivedPacket(RadioPacketProperty.SignalStrength) + 128 as a bar graph out of 100.
  • Resend automatically up to three times before showing the cross.
  • Shake to send a "wave" string that plays a short tune on the other badge.

#Further reading

  • MakeCode Micro Chat project (opens in a new tab): a short official tutorial for a two-board radio chat, good for comparing with your messenger.
  • micro:bit Python Editor guide (opens in a new tab): a tour of the Reference, Ideas, and simulator panels you used for the port.
  • MicroPython radio module (opens in a new tab): the full list of radio.config options, including queue length and transmit power.

What you'll learn

  • Choose the right send and receive pair for a message.
  • Track messages with variables, labels, and timers.
  • Find radio bugs that produce no error message.
  • Translate a small MakeCode radio program into MicroPython.

Every exercise runs in the MakeCode simulator, which shows a second board as soon as you use a radio block. Both boards run the same program, so each exercise is one program that can play either part. Set a group in on start for every exercise; the solutions use 5.

#Warm-up: predict before you press

This program is on both boards. You press A on the top board three times, then B on the bottom board once. What does each board show at the end?

Show solution

The bottom board shows 3; the top board shows nothing. Each A press sends a 1 that only the other board receives (a board never hears its own broadcast), so the bottom board's count climbs to 3 while the top board's stays at 0. B on the bottom board shows its own count.

#Exercise 1: Remote doorbell

Pressing A on either board rings the other: it shows a bell-ish icon (use IconNames.QuarterNote), plays a tone, and clears the screen after a second.

Need a hint?

You need one send (sendString is fine) and its matching receive block. Do the showing, beeping, and clearing in the receiver.

Show solution

Checking for "DING" costs one line now and saves you later, when you add a second kind of string message.

#Exercise 2: Who's been knocking?

The bottom board keeps a count of how many knocks it has received and shows the count after each one. Shaking a board sends a knock. Pressing B resets that board's count to 0.

Need a hint?

Use input.onGesture(Gesture.Shake, ...) to send. In the simulator, a SHAKE button appears on each board once your code uses a gesture.

Show solution

#Exercise 3: Remote weather station

Every two seconds, each board broadcasts its temperature and light level as labelled values. The receiving board remembers the latest of each. Pressing A shows the remote temperature; pressing B shows the remote light level.

Need a hint?

loops.everyInterval(2000, function () { ... }) runs code on a timer. In the receive block, store value in a different variable depending on name.

Show solution

The receiver stores readings and the buttons show them. Splitting "collect" from "show" is a pattern you'll keep using.

#Exercise 4: Three silent bugs

A student flashed the sender program onto one real micro:bit and the receiver program onto another. Nothing ever appears on the receiver, and neither board shows an error. Find all three bugs.

Need a hint?

Check the group, the kind of message, and the label length. Any one of them is enough to keep the receiver dark.

Show solution
  1. The groups are 12 and 21. Make them the same.
  2. The sender sends a value but the receiver only listens for numbers. Use onReceivedValue.
  3. "brightness" has 10 characters and would arrive as brightne. Use a short label.

The sender's line becomes radio.sendValue("light", input.lightLevel()), with the group still 12.

#Exercise 5: Translate the doorbell to MicroPython

Rewrite your Exercise 1 doorbell for python.microbit.org. Test it in that editor's simulator by pressing A (the Radio panel shows what your board sent) and by typing DING into the panel's message box (your board should ring).

Need a hint?

You need a while True loop that checks button_a.was_pressed() and calls radio.receive() on every pass. The note picture is Image.MUSIC_QUAVER, and music.pitch(659, 300) plays the tone after import music.

Show solution

Run this in the Python editor, not desktop Python, where from microbit import * raises an import error.

The two event blocks became two if checks inside one loop. radio.receive() returns None when nothing is waiting, and None == "DING" is simply false, so no extra check is needed.

#Exercise 6: Hot and cold finder

One board is a hidden beacon and the other is a finder. Press A to make a board the beacon: it sends a number every 200 ms. The other board plots a bar graph of the signal strength, so the bars rise as you walk toward the beacon. (The simulator can't model distance, so you need real boards to play; the code still runs there.)

Need a hint?

Signal strength runs from about -128 to about -28. Adding 128 turns that into 0 to 100, which led.plotBarGraph(level, 100) can draw. A variable beacon decides whether the forever loop sends.

Show solution

Walls, bodies, and even which way the board faces change the reading, so expect the bars to jitter. Moving slowly and watching the trend works better than trusting one reading.

#Challenge: Rock, paper, scissors over radio

Shake to pick a random throw (0 rock, 1 paper, 2 scissors), show it, and send it. When a board knows both its own throw and its opponent's, it shows a tick for a win, a cross for a loss, or = for a draw. Press B to play again.

Need a hint?

Keep two variables, mine and theirs, both starting at -1 for "not chosen yet". After any shake or any received throw, call one function that does nothing unless both are 0 or more. With throws as 0, 1, 2, you win exactly when (mine - theirs + 3) % 3 == 1.

Show solution

The return at the top of the shake handler stops a second shake from changing your throw after you've already sent it.

The Science Buddies video below builds a sender and receiver, then makes them two-way and sets a group, which is the same shape as Exercises 1 to 3.

m6-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain why a loop that checks a button can miss presses, and how an event handler catches them.
  • Split a program into short handlers that change variables and one loop that draws.
  • Describe a device's behaviour as states and transitions, and code it with a state variable.
  • Time things with control.millis() instead of long pauses.

Load this counter, press A five times quickly, and watch the number.

You pressed five times. The board probably shows 1, maybe 2. Nothing is broken in the hardware. The program is only looking at the button for an instant in every pass of the loop, and the rest of each pass is spent scrolling a number and pausing. A quick tap that starts and ends during the pause never happens, as far as this code knows.

#Polling: checking over and over

Code that keeps asking "is it happening yet?" is polling. It's like checking your phone every hour for a message: fine for a letter that sits there until you look, useless for a doorbell that rings for half a second.

Polling works when two things are true: you check often, and the thing you're checking lasts longer than the gap between checks. A tap on a button lasts roughly a tenth of a second. The loop above checks about once every second and a bit. The numbers don't line up, so presses fall through the gaps.

#Events: let the micro:bit tell you

The fix is to stop asking and let the board tell you. An event handler is a block of code you hand to the micro:bit in advance: "when A is pressed, run this." Here is the same counter, written with events:

Five quick presses now give 5. The display may lag while a number scrolls, but the count is right, and the next pass of the loop catches up.

What changed? Behind the scenes MakeCode runs a small scheduler. According to MakeCode's own explanation of the micro:bit as a reactive system, it checks the buttons and other inputs every 6 milliseconds, far faster than any tap, and lines up your handler to run for each press it finds. You still have polling, but it's fast polling done by the system, so your code doesn't have to.

#Short handlers, one loop that draws

The scheduler can only run one piece of your code at a time. Handlers and the forever loop take turns, and they hand over control whenever they pause or finish (a forever loop also pauses briefly at the end of each pass). That has two practical consequences:

  • Keep handlers short. A handler that scrolls a long message makes the device feel laggy while it runs. Change a variable and get out.
  • Draw in one place. If two handlers both write to the LEDs, their images can overwrite each other halfway through. Let handlers update variables and let one forever loop decide what the screen shows.

The event version of the counter already follows both rules: the handler adds one, the loop draws.

#States: what is the device doing right now?

A kitchen timer has a problem a counter doesn't. Pressing B should start the timer when it's idle, pause it while it's running, and resume it when paused. The same event needs a different reaction depending on what the device is currently doing.

That "currently doing" is called the state. List every state the device can be in, then list which events move it from one state to another. Those moves are transitions. A state diagram puts both on one picture:

Each box is a state; each arrow is labelled with the event that causes it. An event with no arrow out of the current state does nothing. Pressing A while running, for example, has no arrow, so it's ignored.

In code, the state is one variable, and each handler checks it before acting:

Here's the same machine as a short Python model, fed a list of events instead of real buttons. Step through it and watch state change only when the event matches an arrow in the diagram.

The first A arrives while the timer is idle, so the state stays IDLE. The second A arrives while paused and is ignored too. Only events that match an arrow do anything.

#Measuring time without freezing

The timer still needs to know when time is up. The tempting way is basic.pause(60000). But a paused loop can't update the display, can't notice the B button changed the state to paused, and can't stop early. It's the polling problem again, in a new costume.

Instead, write down when something started and keep comparing with the clock. control.millis() gives the milliseconds since the board started:

The bar graph fills over ten seconds and then shows a tick. Press A at any moment and it starts again at once, because nothing is ever stuck in a pause. "Remember the start, compare with now" is the pattern behind every timer, alarm, and timeout you'll write.

#Mistakes that break state machines

⚠️ Watch out

if where you meant else if. This looks like a pause button:

Press B while running: the first if sets PAUSED, then the second if sees PAUSED and sets it straight back. The timer never pauses. Fix: chain the checks with else if, so one press makes at most one transition.

⚠️ Watch out

A typo in a state name. if (state == "RUNING") is never true and MakeCode won't warn you, because any text is a valid string. Fix: copy and paste state names, or in JavaScript use numbered states with named variables such as let RUNNING = 1.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1The polling counter at the top of this lesson shows 2 after five fast presses. Why?

  • The hardware can register far more than that; the code just isn't looking.

  • Polling catches a tap only if the tap overlaps the moment of the check.

  • It adds one every time it runs; the problem is how rarely it runs.

Show answer

B. Polling catches a tap only if the tap overlaps the moment of the check.

2The timer is in the Running state. According to the state diagram, what does pressing A do?

  • That arrow starts from Ringing, not Running.

  • Events without a matching transition from the current state are ignored.

  • Pausing is triggered by B, not A.

Show answer

B. Events without a matching transition from the current state are ignored.

3You want an LED to turn on ten minutes after a button press, while the board keeps responding to other buttons. Which approach fits?

  • While that handler waits, you can't cancel it or show progress, and it ties up its slot for ten minutes.

  • Comparing with a saved start time never blocks, so everything else keeps working.

  • The problem is waiting, not detecting the press.

Show answer

B. Comparing with a saved start time never blocks, so everything else keeps working.

Key takeaways

  • Polling asks "is it happening?" over and over and misses anything shorter than the gap between checks.
  • Event handlers run when something happens; MakeCode's scheduler watches the inputs for you every few milliseconds.
  • Handlers change variables; one forever loop draws. Keep handlers short.
  • A state machine lists what the device can be doing and which events move it on. In code it's a state variable checked with if/else if.
  • For timing, save a start time with control.millis() and compare, rather than pausing.

#Further reading

  • The micro:bit: a reactive system (opens in a new tab): MakeCode's own explanation of the scheduler, why forever pauses, and how handlers take turns.
  • Event handlers in MakeCode (opens in a new tab): what counts as an event and how handlers are registered.
  • State, from Game Programming Patterns (opens in a new tab): a free, friendly chapter showing how state machines tame messy game code.

m6-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Turn a state diagram into a working MakeCode program, one state at a time.
  • Count down with a saved end time instead of basic.pause.
  • Pause and resume a timer without losing time.
  • Test every transition in the simulator with a checklist.

You're building a timer for things like brushing your teeth or a study sprint. Button A adds five seconds. Button B starts it, pauses it, and resumes it. When the time runs out it flashes and beeps until you press a button. Shaking it cancels whatever it's doing. Here's the whole design before any code:

Every arrow becomes a few lines of code. Every state becomes one branch of the forever loop that draws the screen. Work in the JavaScript view at makecode.microbit.org and run the simulator after each step.

#Step 1: A state variable and a loop that draws it

Start with the variables and the Setting state only. total is how many seconds the timer is set to.

The simulator shows 0. Nothing else happens yet, which is right: no handler can change anything.

#Step 2: Add time with button A

A handler checks the state before acting. In Setting, A adds five seconds, capped at 60 so a stray press can't set ten minutes by accident.

Press A three times quickly. The display might still be scrolling the old number, but when it catches up it shows 15. The handler counted every press; only the drawing lagged. That's the event-driven split from the Notes lesson doing its job.

#Step 3: Start with B and count down

When B starts the timer, the code doesn't count seconds one by one. It works out when the timer should end, in board time, and stores it:

Then the drawing loop gets a Running branch that compares the end time with the clock on every pass:

Set 15 seconds and press B. The bar graph shrinks for the first few seconds, then single digits count down from 9. Single digits fit on the 5×5 screen without scrolling, which is why the code switches to numbers only near the end. Math.ceil rounds up, so 2.3 seconds left shows as 3, the way a real timer does.

📝 Note

The total > 0 check stops B from starting a timer set to zero. Every arrow in the diagram with a condition in brackets becomes an && in code.

#Step 4: Ring when time is up

"Time is up" isn't a button, so no handler catches it. The forever loop notices it while drawing the Running state and makes the transition itself. Add the check before the drawing, and a Ringing branch that flashes and beeps:

Each pass of the Ringing branch is one flash and one beep. The short pause here is fine, because ringing is the one time the loop has nothing else to watch. Now let A and B stop the alarm by adding a Ringing branch to each handler:

Do the same in B's handler with else if (state == "RINGING"). Set five seconds, start it, and let it ring. A press brings you back to Setting with the same total, ready to go again.

#Step 5: Pause and resume without losing time

Pausing is where the end-time idea pays off. When you pause, save how many milliseconds were left. When you resume, set a new end time that far into the future:

Here's that arithmetic on its own, with made-up clock readings. Step through and watch remaining survive a 22-second pause.

Eight seconds had passed, so twelve were left, and twelve are still left after the break. Without saving remaining, resuming would use the old endTime, which is already in the past, and the timer would ring the instant you resumed.

Give Paused something to show in the drawing loop, a classic pause symbol:

In the finished program this becomes one more else if branch in the main loop rather than a second forever.

#Step 6: Shake to cancel

One handler, no conditions needed: from any state, shaking returns to Setting. In the simulator, a SHAKE button appears on the board once your code uses a gesture.

#The finished program

Now test every arrow in the diagram, not just the happy path. Tick each row off in the simulator:

Do this You should see
Press B with the total at 0 Still 0; nothing starts
A three times, then B Bars shrink, then 9 down to 1
B while running, wait 10 s, B again Pause bars, then the countdown continues from where it stopped
Let it reach zero Flashing target and beeps
A or B while ringing Back to the total you set
SHAKE while running or paused Back to the total you set
A while running Nothing changes (no arrow for it)

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the timer store endTime instead of looping basic.pause(1000) and subtracting one each time?

  • It works; the trouble is what it costs.

  • Comparing the clock with a saved end time takes no waiting at all, and pausing becomes simple arithmetic.

  • Accuracy isn't the point; staying responsive is.

Show answer

B. Comparing the clock with a saved end time takes no waiting at all, and pausing becomes simple arithmetic.

2You remove the line remaining = endTime - control.millis() from the pause branch. What happens when you resume?

  • remaining would still be 0 from the start, so resuming can't work normally.

  • With remaining stuck at 0, endTime becomes the current time and left drops to 0 on the next pass.

  • Nothing in the resume branch reads total.

Show answer

B. With remaining stuck at 0, endTime becomes the current time and left drops to 0 on the next pass.

3Where does the Running to Ringing transition happen, and why there?

  • A stops the alarm after it rings; something else has to start it.

  • Not every transition comes from a button. Time-based ones belong wherever the clock is checked.

  • Shake only cancels; it never starts the alarm.

Show answer

B. Not every transition comes from a button. Time-based ones belong wherever the clock is checked.

Key takeaways

  • Draw the state diagram first; each arrow becomes one if/else if branch in a handler, and each state becomes a branch of the drawing loop.
  • Count down with a saved end time and control.millis(), never a chain of pauses.
  • To pause a timer, save what's left; to resume, set a new end time that far ahead.
  • Time-based transitions happen in the loop that watches the clock.
  • Test every arrow, including the "nothing should happen" ones.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Make A add 5 seconds, but touch the logo (V2's input.onLogoEvent(TouchButtonEvent.Pressed, ...)) to add a whole minute.
  • Send radio.sendString("DONE") when the timer rings, so a second board across the room alerts you too.
  • Add a "snooze" arrow from Ringing: B sets a new end time 10 seconds ahead instead of going back to Setting.
  • Replace the scrolling total in Setting with a bar graph so the display never lags.

  • plot bar graph reference (opens in a new tab): how the bar graph scales a value against a maximum, used here for the long part of the countdown.

What you'll learn

  • Tell polling code from event-driven code at a glance.
  • Model devices and games as states, then code them with a state variable.
  • Use control.millis() for stopwatches, delays, and random timings.
  • Find bugs caused by pausing inside a handler.

Each exercise is a fresh MakeCode project. For the state exercises, sketch the states and arrows on paper before you write code; it takes two minutes and saves twenty.

#Warm-up: polling or events?

Which of these will count every quick press of A, and which will miss some?

Show solution

Only snippet 2 counts every press, because it's an event handler. Snippets 1 and 3 poll. Snippet 3 checks just once every two seconds, so it misses almost everything. Snippet 1 checks often, but it stops checking whenever a two-digit score is scrolling, and a long hold counts several times because the loop sees the button still down on the next pass.

#Exercise 1: A people counter that doesn't lie

This counter for a club door misses people and sometimes counts one person twice. Rewrite it so every press of A counts exactly once, and pressing B resets the count to zero.

Need a hint?

Move the counting into input.onButtonPressed. The forever loop should only draw.

Show solution

onButtonPressed fires once per press-and-release, so a long hold counts as one person, and the scheduler catches taps even while a number scrolls.

#Exercise 2: A three-way lamp

Button A cycles the lamp through off, dim, and bright, then back to off. When on, every LED lights up.

Need a hint?

Use numbers for the states: 0 off, 1 dim, 2 bright. (lamp + 1) % 3 moves to the next one. led.setBrightness takes 0 to 255.

Show solution

The handler only changes the state; the loop turns the state into light. Adding a fourth mode means changing % 3 to % 4 and adding one branch.

#Exercise 3: Stopwatch

Press A to start; press A again to stop and show the time in seconds with one decimal place. Press B to reset, but only when the stopwatch is stopped.

Need a hint?

Three states: READY, RUNNING, STOPPED. Save control.millis() when you start, and work out elapsed when you stop. Math.round(elapsed / 100) / 10 gives one decimal place.

Show solution

B does nothing while running because there's no RUNNING branch in its handler. Deciding what not to respond to is half of state design.

#Exercise 4: Read a program, draw its states

Draw the state diagram for this bike alarm. List every state and label every arrow with its event.

Need a hint?

B has no if, so it works from every state. Shake only does something in one state.

Show solution

There's no arrow from Off on shake, so bumping a disarmed bike does nothing, and no arrow from Alarm on A, so a thief pressing A can't silence it.

#Exercise 5: The alarm that arms itself after you cancel it

The owner wants a ten-second delay after pressing A so they can walk away. A student added a pause. Now if you press A and then B within ten seconds, the alarm shows "off" and arms anyway a few seconds later. Explain the bug and fix it.

Need a hint?

While A's handler sleeps, B's handler runs and sets OFF. Then A's handler wakes up and carries on with the next line. Give the delay its own state and let a loop finish it.

Show solution

The paused handler doesn't know the world changed while it slept; it blindly runs state = "ARMED". The fix is an ARMING state with a saved time, checked by the forever loop:

Now B during the delay moves the state to OFF, and the loop's check for ARMING is simply false from then on.

#Exercise 6: Red light, green light

Build the playground game for one player. Press B to start. While the light is green (show a bar graph of your progress), each press of A is a step. The light flips between green and red at random times, one to three seconds apart; red shows a cross. Pressing A on red puts you out (skull). Reach 20 steps to win (happy face). B starts a new game after a win or a loss.

Need a hint?

States: READY, GREEN, RED, OUT, WIN. Store switchAt = control.millis() + randint(1000, 3000). In the forever loop, if the state is GREEN or RED and the time has passed, flip the colour and pick a new switchAt.

Show solution

Try making it fairer: ignore a press on red if it arrives within 200 ms of the switch, since nobody reacts that fast. That's one more condition using the time you saved in switchAt.

#Challenge: Hot potato over radio

Two boards on the same group. Pressing B on one board starts a game: it picks a secret fuse of 5 to 15 seconds and becomes the holder. The holder shows a diamond and must shake to throw the potato to the other board, which becomes the holder for the rest of the fuse. Whoever is holding when the fuse runs out shows a skull and tells the other board, which shows a happy face.

Need a hint?

Each board's control.millis() counts from when that board started, so you can't send an end time from one board to the other. Send the time remaining instead, radio.sendValue("potato", explodeAt - control.millis()), and let the catcher add it to its own clock.

Show solution

The game would be unplayable if each board kept its own fuse; sending the remaining time is what makes one fuse burn across two devices.

What you'll learn

  • Plan a log: the question, the columns, how often to sample, and for how long.
  • Record rows with the data logger extension on a micro:bit V2 (or in the simulator).
  • Get the log off the board as a CSV file.
  • Read a CSV in Python, summarise it, and chart it to spot a pattern.

At 10:00 the micro:bit on the windowsill says 21 °C. Is that warm? Is the room heating up or cooling down? Is the window warmer than the door? One number can't answer any of those. Twenty-one readings taken thirty seconds apart can, and by the end of this lesson you'll read a log like that and find something in it you couldn't have seen live.

#Plan the log before you press start

Data logging means recording measurements over time, so you can study them later. The micro:bit V2 can store a table of readings in its own memory, and it keeps them even when the battery is unplugged. Before you write any code, answer four questions:

  1. What's the question? "Does sunlight on the windowsill warm the board, and how fast?" is a question. "Collect temperature" isn't.
  2. What columns do you need? Here: temperature and light level. The logger adds a time column for you.
  3. How often? Fast enough to catch the change you care about. Sunlight warming a room changes over minutes, so every 30 seconds is plenty. A falling object changes in milliseconds and would need much faster logging.
  4. For how long? Long enough to see the whole change, plus a little before and after.

Multiply it out before you start: logging every 30 seconds for 10 minutes gives 600 ÷ 30 = 20 readings, plus the first one at time zero, so 21 rows. Every 10 seconds for a whole school day would give thousands. The log's space is limited, so a sensible interval is part of the plan.

#Record rows with the data logger

Logging lives in an extension. In MakeCode, click Extensions in the block list, search for datalogger, and add it. It needs a micro:bit V2; on a V1 board the program stops with error code 927. This program logs temperature and light every 30 seconds, and button A starts and stops it:

Line by line:

  • includeTimestamp(...Seconds) adds a Time (seconds) column to every row automatically.
  • setColumnTitles fixes the column names and their order before the first row is written. Do it once, at the start.
  • createCV("temperature", ...) pairs a column name with a value ("CV" means column-value), and datalogger.log writes one row made of those pairs.
  • loops.everyInterval(30000, ...) runs every 30 seconds, and the logging flag decides whether a row is written. The heart tells you, from across the room, that logging is on.
  • onLogFull runs when there's no space left. Stopping and showing a cross is much better than silently losing data.

In the simulator, press A, drag the thermometer and the light control around, and click Show data under the simulator to watch the rows appear. Shorten the interval to 1000 while testing so you aren't waiting half a minute per row.

#Get the log off the board

Real micro:bit V2

  1. Plug the micro:bit into a computer with a USB cable. It appears as a drive called MICROBIT.
  2. Open the MY_DATA file on that drive. It opens in your web browser as a table of your rows.
  3. Click Download to save the table as a CSV file. Copy puts it on the clipboard for a spreadsheet, and the visual preview draws a quick chart in the page.

Simulator

  1. Run the program and log a few rows.
  2. Click Show data under the simulator to open the data view.
  3. Use the download button above the chart to save the data as a file on your computer.

CSV means comma-separated values: a plain text file with one row per line and commas between the columns. Every spreadsheet can open it, and so can Python. A log from the windowsill experiment starts like this:

#Read the CSV in Python

The next cell writes that file to disk, standing in for the CSV you'd download. It holds ten minutes of readings, and partway through, a patch of sunlight reached the windowsill.

Now read it the way you'd read any downloaded log. csv.DictReader turns each line into a dictionary keyed by the header, so row["light"] is that row's light reading, as text. That's why each value goes through float or int before any maths.

The summary says the temperature went from 21 to 24 and the light from about 40 to almost 190. It doesn't say when, or which changed first. A chart does:

The light changes in one step, between 270 and 300 seconds. The temperature doesn't move at that moment; it creeps up over the next five minutes. You'd never notice that lag standing next to the board, but it's obvious once the readings sit on one time axis.

#Noise, lag, and what a log can't tell you

Look at 120 seconds: the temperature reads 22, then drops back to 21. Nothing in the room changed. Sensors jitter by a step or so, and a single bump isn't a trend. Two habits help: look for changes that last several rows, and compare averages of a few readings rather than single values. The next cell finds the moment the light changed most, then the first time the temperature reached 23:

About two and a half minutes passed between the light arriving and the temperature reaching 23. One more thing to keep in mind: the micro:bit measures temperature with a sensor inside its processor, so direct sun on the board warms the chip itself. That makes it a fine detector of "the sun is on me" and a rougher measure of the air in the room. Knowing what your sensor actually measures is part of reading the data honestly.

#Mistakes that cost you your data

⚠️ Watch out

Flashing new code before copying your data. Downloading a new program to the micro:bit clears the log so it can start fresh. Fix: open MY_DATA and download the CSV first, then change the program.

⚠️ Watch out

Changing column names halfway. A row logged with createCV("temp", ...) after the header says temperature creates a new column, and the MY_DATA page splits into separate sections. Fix: set all the column titles once at the start and copy the names exactly.

⚠️ Watch out

Reading the time column as a clock. Time (seconds) counts from when the board last reset, not the time of day. Pressing reset or swapping batteries starts it at zero again. Fix: write down the real start time in your notes.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1You log every 15 seconds for 2 hours. About how many rows will the log have?

  • That's one row per minute; every 15 seconds is four rows per minute.

  • 2 hours is 7,200 seconds, and 7,200 ÷ 15 = 480 (plus the first row at time zero).

  • That would be one row every second.

Show answer

B. 2 hours is 7,200 seconds, and 7,200 ÷ 15 = 480 (plus the first row at time zero).

2You fix a small bug and click Download to flash the new program, then open MY_DATA to grab yesterday's readings. What do you find?

  • Flashing a new program marks the old log as erased.

  • Always copy the CSV before you change the program on the board.

  • The rows themselves are gone from the MY_DATA view, not just renumbered.

Show answer

B. Always copy the CSV before you change the program on the board.

3In the windowsill log, light jumped at 300 s and the temperature climbed from about 360 s. Which conclusion does the data support?

  • The data shows the order and the delay. It's one run, so you'd repeat it before claiming a general rule.

  • The chart shows the light changing in one step and the temperature lagging by minutes.

  • The sensor sits in the processor, so sunlight on the board can warm the chip more than the air.

Show answer

A. The data shows the order and the delay. It's one run, so you'd repeat it before claiming a general rule.

Key takeaways

  • Plan before logging: question, columns, interval, duration. Work out the row count up front.
  • The data logger writes rows of column-value pairs with datalogger.log(datalogger.createCV(...)); set column titles and the timestamp once, at the start.
  • On a V2, MY_DATA on the MICROBIT drive downloads the log as a CSV. In the simulator, use Show data.
  • A chart on a shared time axis shows order and lag that a summary can't.
  • Single bumps are noise; trends last several rows. Know what your sensor really measures.

#Further reading

  • micro:bit data logging guide (opens in a new tab): the official guide to planning a log, reading MY_DATA, timestamps, and erasing.
  • MakeCode datalogger reference (opens in a new tab): every data logger block, with examples of column titles and timestamps.
  • Python's csv module (opens in a new tab): the reference for DictReader and friends, for when your logs get bigger.

What you'll learn

  • Write one program that can play several roles, chosen with a button at start-up.
  • Send labelled readings from numbered stations to a hub over radio.
  • Stream readings to the computer with serial.writeValue and log them with the data logger.
  • Detect a silent network with a timeout, and analyse the hub's log in Python.

Here's the network you're building. Every board gets the same program. Press A at start-up and a board becomes a station: it measures the temperature every five seconds and broadcasts it with its station number. Press B and it becomes the hub: it listens, streams every reading to the computer, writes it to the data log, and shows a cross if nothing has arrived for 15 seconds.

Why one program for every role? In a classroom you flash the same file to 30 boards, which is far easier than keeping track of three different programs. In the MakeCode simulator you have no choice anyway: both simulated boards always run the same code.

#Step 1: Pick a role at start-up

The board starts with no role and shows ?. The first press decides. On a station, later presses of A pick the station number, from 1 to 9 and round again.

This is a state machine with three states (NONE, STATION, HUB) and no way back, which is what you want: a hub that turned into a station mid-experiment would ruin the log. Press A on the top simulated board and B on the bottom one. The top board shows 1, the bottom one a house.

#Step 2: Stations broadcast a labelled reading

Each station sends its temperature every five seconds with a label like s1 or s2. The label is short (well under the 8-character limit) and carries the station number, so the hub knows who sent what.

led.toggle(4, 0) flips the top-right LED on each send, a small heartbeat that tells you the station is alive without hiding its number.

#Step 3: The hub streams readings to the computer

serial.writeValue(name, value) sends a line like s1:21 over the USB cable. MakeCode's Show data view reads those lines and draws a live chart, with one line per name.

Two checks guard the handler. role == "HUB" stops stations from reacting to each other's messages, since they hear them too. name.charAt(0) == "s" ignores any other value messages that might share the group.

Run it: make the top board station 1 and the bottom board the hub. After a few seconds, Show data appears under the simulator. Click it and you'll see an s1 line. Drag the station's thermometer up and the line climbs five seconds later.

📝 Note

With a real micro:bit as the hub, the same chart works once MakeCode is paired with the board over USB (WebUSB, in Chrome or Edge). The data view then lists the micro:bit as its source instead of the simulator.

#Step 4: The hub writes every reading to the log

The live chart vanishes when you close the editor. The data logger keeps the readings on the hub itself, ready to download as a CSV later. Set the columns when the board becomes the hub, not at start-up, because stations might be older V1 boards, which stop with error 927 if they touch the log:

Then add one line to the hub's receive handler, after serial.writeValue:

Each row now holds the time, the station label, and the reading. Storing the label in its own column (instead of one column per station) means the table never needs to change shape when a tenth station joins.

#Step 5: Warn when the network goes quiet

A hub that shows a happy house while every station's battery has died is lying to you. The hub already records lastHeard; a forever loop compares it with the clock. A quiet flag makes sure the screen only changes when the situation changes, so the loop isn't redrawing the house fifty times a second.

That's a two-state machine (listening, quiet) driven by time, the same pattern as the countdown timer.

#Step 6: Test the network

Do this You should see
A on top board, B on bottom board Top shows 1; bottom shows a house
Wait 10 seconds Top's corner LED blinks; hub's centre LED flickers; Show data appears
Drag the station's thermometer The s1 line in Show data moves within 5 s
Press A twice more on the station It shows 3, and a new s3 line starts in the chart
Restart, make the bottom board the hub, never choose a station role After 15 s the hub shows a cross

#The finished program

#Read the hub's log in Python

Suppose a class ran this for 20 minutes with stations on the windowsill (s1), by the door (s2), and on a desk (s3), each reporting every two minutes to keep the file short. The first cell saves the CSV you'd download from the hub's MY_DATA page. Notice the times don't line up: each station started on its own, so its readings arrive a couple of seconds apart from the others.

Because the station is a column, the first job is to split the rows into one list per station. A dictionary keyed by the label does it in a few lines:

The window station ranged five degrees, the door station dipped and recovered, and the desk barely moved. Put them on one chart to see when:

Now the pattern is plain. The window warms steadily from about 600 seconds, which fits the sun moving onto the sill. The door drops three degrees around 720 to 840 seconds and recovers, which looks like a door opened to a cold corridor. The desk, in the middle of the room, hardly notices either. No single board could have told you that the room isn't one temperature; three boards and one hub could.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the board choose its role with a button press instead of using two separate programs?

  • It can; you'd just have to keep track of which board got which.

  • Choosing the role at run time keeps a whole class on one file and makes the simulator test realistic.

  • Radio only needs a shared group and matching message kinds.

Show answer

B. Choosing the role at run time keeps a whole class on one file and makes the simulator test realistic.

2Stations send sendValue("s" + station, ...). What would go wrong if every station sent sendValue("temp", ...) instead?

  • Every message would look the same, so the window, door, and desk readings would blur into one column of numbers.

  • The messages would still arrive; they'd just carry no identity.

  • temp has 4 characters, so it fits.

Show answer

A. Every message would look the same, so the window, door, and desk readings would blur into one column of numbers.

3The hub shows a cross. What do you know for sure?

  • That's one explanation, but not the only one.

  • The cross reports a fact about the hub. The cause (range, batteries, wrong group, no stations chosen) is yours to investigate.

  • A full log is reported by the data logger, not by this timeout.

Show answer

B. The cross reports a fact about the hub. The cause (range, batteries, wrong group, no stations chosen) is yours to investigate.

Key takeaways

  • One program with a role chosen at start-up scales from two simulated boards to a whole classroom.
  • Put the sender's identity in the label (s1, s2) so the hub can tell readings apart.
  • serial.writeValue gives a live chart in Show data; the data logger keeps a CSV on the hub for later.
  • A timeout on "last heard" turns silence into a visible warning.
  • Store the station as a column, then group by it in Python to compare stations on one time axis.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Send light level too, as l1, l2…, and log it in a third column.
  • Have the hub reply radio.sendValue("ok", station) so each station can show a tick when its reading arrives, like the mood messenger's receipt.
  • Track lastHeard per station in an array, so the hub can say which station went quiet.
  • Add a threshold alarm: the hub beeps if any station reads above 28 °C.

#Further reading

  • Remote data collection (opens in a new tab): MakeCode's guide to radio senders and a USB-connected receiver, including stations identified by serial number.
  • Viewing your data (opens in a new tab): what each control in the Show data view does, including the download button.
