What you'll learn

  • Choose a logging interval and predict how many rows it produces.
  • Log button-press events with the data logger.
  • Read, clean, and summarise CSV logs in Python.
  • Chart logs to compare stations and count events over time.

Exercise 1 is MakeCode; the rest are Python, working on logs shaped exactly like the ones a micro:bit's MY_DATA page downloads. Every Python solution runs on its own, with the log typed in at the top, so you can paste any of them into a Python editor and change the data.

#Warm-up: read a log by eye

How often was this logged, what happened at 20 seconds, and how do you know it wasn't someone switching on a light?

Show solution

Every 10 seconds (the time goes up by 10 each row). At 20 seconds the sound level jumped from about 14 to 96 for a single reading, so something loud and short happened, like a door slamming. The light column didn't change, so it wasn't a lamp.

#Exercise 1: Traffic survey logger

Make a counter for a traffic survey outside school. Pressing A logs a car and B logs a bike. Each press writes one row with a vehicle column, and the board shows a quick icon so the counter knows the press registered.

Need a hint?

Set the timestamp and the column title once at the start. In each button handler, datalogger.log(datalogger.createCV("vehicle", "car")). A column value can be text as well as a number.

Show solution

This log isn't taken on a timer; each row is an event. The timestamps are what let you count vehicles per minute later (Exercise 6).

#Exercise 2: Pick a sensible interval

How many rows does each plan produce? Write a function rows(duration_s, interval_s) that counts the first reading at time zero, then use it for all three.

  1. Fridge door test: every 1 second for 5 minutes.
  2. Plant shelf: every 10 minutes for 1 week.
  3. Bike ride: every 0.1 seconds for 20 minutes.
Need a hint?

Readings happen at 0, interval, 2 × interval, and so on, up to the duration. That's duration ÷ interval readings, plus one for time zero. Use round(duration / interval) rather than //: 0.1 can't be stored exactly in binary, and 1200 // 0.1 gives 11999.0.

Show solution

The plant shelf needs only about a thousand rows for a whole week, but the bike ride generates over ten thousand in 20 minutes. Fast logging fills the log quickly, so only log fast when the thing you're measuring changes fast.

#Exercise 3: How loud was lunch?

A sound logger ran in the cafeteria, one reading every 5 seconds. Print the number of readings, the average, the loudest reading, and how many readings were above 100.

Need a hint?

Read with csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(log)) so you can keep the log in a string. Convert each sound value with int before doing maths.

Show solution

io.StringIO makes a string behave like an open file, which is handy for testing before you have a real download.

#Exercise 4: Clean a messy log

This temperature log has two problems that real logs often have: one reading is blank, and the header appears a second time in the middle because the board was reset during logging. Skip anything that isn't a number, then print how many good readings remain and their average.

Need a hint?

Use the plain csv.reader so the repeated header comes through as an ordinary row. A value is usable if value.strip().lstrip("-").isdigit() is true.

Show solution

The check throws away the header rows (temperature isn't a number) and the blank. Notice the times restart at 0 after the reset: if you needed real times, you'd have to stitch the two sections together using your own notes.

#Exercise 5: Which corner is warmer?

Two stations logged to a hub. Plot both on one chart with a legend, then print each station's average. Which corner is warmer, and from what time?

Need a hint?

Group rows into a dictionary keyed by station, like the build-along. Call plt.plot once per station with label= and finish with plt.legend().

Show solution

The south corner averages warmer, but the chart tells the better story: the corners stay within a degree of each other until about 240 seconds, then the south one climbs. An average alone would hide when the difference started.

#Exercise 6: Cars and bikes per minute

Using a traffic survey log like Exercise 1's, count cars and bikes in each minute and draw a grouped bar chart.

Need a hint?

The minute for a row is int(time // 60). Keep two lists of counts, one per vehicle, with one slot per minute.

Show solution

Shifting the bars by 0.2 either side of each minute puts cars and bikes next to each other instead of on top of each other.

#The trick for the challenge: count a step once, even if it wobbles

A footstep shows up in an acceleration log as a spike well above the resting value of about 1000. Real spikes wobble: the reading can shoot up, dip a little, and shoot up again within the same step. A counter that adds one every time the reading crosses a line will count that wobble twice. The fix is two lines instead of one: count a step when the reading rises above a high line, and only get ready for the next step once it falls below a lower line.

A dip to 1200 in the middle of a step doesn't reach 1100, so the counter stays in Stepping and doesn't count again.

#Challenge: A step counter that ignores bounces

The list below is acceleration strength logged 10 times a second during a short walk. Count steps two ways: the naive way (add one every time the reading goes from 1500 or less to above 1500) and the two-threshold way from the diagram. Print both counts.

Need a hint?

For the two-threshold count, keep a variable ready = True. When ready and the reading is above 1500, count and set ready = False. When the reading is below 1100, set ready = True.

Show solution

The naive counter sees the dip to 1180 in the third step and counts that step twice. The two-threshold counter stays in Stepping until the reading truly settles, so it finds the four steps that were really taken. The same idea, called hysteresis, keeps thermostats from clicking on and off every second.

What you'll learn

  • Explain what the capstone network must do and how each requirement will be checked.
  • Choose a project idea that fits your time, skills, and equipment.
  • Design the radio messages as a protocol table before coding.
  • Draw a state diagram for each role and plan the data your network records.
  • Write a safety plan and a milestone schedule.

A teacher asks the class to vote by raising hands. Twenty-eight hands go up, she counts twenty-seven, and nobody can check. Now picture the same vote on micro:bits: everyone presses A or B, every vote is counted exactly once, a voter whose vote didn't get through sees a cross and can try again, and every poll is saved to a CSV for later. That's a connected invention: several devices, each with a job, talking by radio to do something one device couldn't.

Your capstone is a network like that. You can build it entirely in the MakeCode simulator, which shows two boards whenever you use radio, or on real micro:bits if you have them. This lesson is all planning. It feels slower than coding, but networks are where unplanned projects fall apart: two boards that disagree about what a message means fail silently, and you lose an afternoon finding out why.

#The brief

Your network must do all of these. The right-hand column is how you'll prove it when you present.

Requirement How you'll show it
At least two roles that talk by radio on a group you chose Demo with two simulated (or real) boards
Inputs handled with events, not polling Point to the event blocks in your code
At least one state machine with three or more states A state diagram that matches the code
Records data (data logger or serial) and you analyse it A CSV plus a chart or summary in Python or a spreadsheet
Visible feedback when a message is lost or a device goes quiet Demo the failure on purpose
Tested, with safety notes and design documentation Your test table and README

#Six project ideas, from gentle to ambitious

Pick one, or invent your own that meets the brief. The stars are a rough guide to how much new thinking each needs beyond this course.

Idea Difficulty Roles Data it records
Hot potato tournament ★ player, scoreboard who exploded, after how long
Classroom voting system ★★ teacher, voter votes per poll
Relay race timer ★★ start gate, finish gate lap times
Climate network with alerts ★★ station, hub readings per station
Quiet-zone sound monitor ★★★ zone sensor, desk display sound levels per zone
Plant care network ★★★ plant sensor, gardener's badge soil moisture over days

Hot potato tournament. Extend the challenge from the event-driven practice: a third role, the scoreboard, hears every BOOM and keeps score across rounds, logging each round's fuse length and loser.

Classroom voting system. A teacher board opens and closes polls; voter boards send A or B. The hard parts are counting each voter once and telling a voter when their vote didn't arrive. The next lesson builds this one step by step as the worked example, so it's the safest choice if you want a guide.

Relay race timer. The start gate sends GO when a button is pressed; the finish gate measures time from hearing GO until a runner breaks the "beam" (a button, or a tilt of the board). Each board's clock starts at a different moment, so the finish gate must time everything with its own control.millis().

Climate network with alerts. Build on the sensor network from Module 7: per-station "last heard" times, a temperature threshold, and an alert the hub sends back to the station that's too warm.

Quiet-zone sound monitor. Stations in different parts of a library send input.soundLevel() (micro:bit V2, 0 to 255). The display board shows which zone is loudest. You'll need averages, because a single cough shouldn't trigger the "too loud" warning.

Plant care network. Needs real hardware: two nails in a plant pot, wired with crocodile clips to pin 1 and 3V, read with pins.analogReadPin(AnalogPin.P1) (wetter soil conducts better and reads higher). The sensor board reports moisture every ten minutes; the gardener's badge lights up when a plant is dry. Add pins.digitalWritePin(DigitalPin.P0, 1) on the badge to switch on an external LED. In the simulator you can still build it, because the simulated board lets you change the pin's reading.

#Design the messages first

Before any code, write down every message your devices will send. This table is your protocol: the agreement every board has to follow. Here is the voting system's:

Message Kind From → to Meaning
OPEN string teacher → voters a poll has started; voting allowed
CLOSED string teacher → voters the poll has ended
A = voter id value voter → teacher a vote for A from this voter
B = voter id value voter → teacher a vote for B from this voter
ack = voter id value teacher → voters receipt: this voter's vote was counted

Check your table against what you already know about micro:bit radio. Every label fits in 8 characters, every string in 19. Each kind of message has one receive block per board, so the table tells you what goes in each if. And every message that matters has a reply, because the sender can't otherwise know it arrived.

#Draw the states for each role

Each role gets its own state diagram. The voter's is the interesting one:

Drawing it exposed questions you'd otherwise meet as bugs: What if a voter presses B after voting A? (No arrow from Done, so nothing happens.) What if CLOSED arrives while a vote is still being resent? (Add an arrow from Sent to Waiting.) Answer each question on the diagram, then code what you drew.

#Plan the data

Decide what question your data will answer, then what to record. For the voting system: "How do class opinions change over a week of polls, and how many voters take part?" That needs one row per poll with the poll number, the two totals, and the number of voters. Write the column names down now and use exactly those names in setColumnTitles.

#Your planning sheet

Copy this into a document or your notebook and fill in every line before you start building.

#Safety plan

Even a simulator-only project gets a safety section, because someone may build your design on real boards. Include the points that apply:

  • Handle micro:bits by their edges, and power them only from the USB cable or the battery pack meant for them.
  • Use batteries of the same type and age in a pack, and never let crocodile clips or wires touch both ends of a battery.
  • Keep boards and battery packs away from water and plant pots' drip trays; a sensor in soil is fine, a board in a puddle isn't.
  • Never connect a micro:bit to mains electricity or to anything plugged into the wall other than a computer's USB port.
  • For devices worn or carried while moving (relay race), secure cables so nobody trips.
  • Radio messages are readable by anyone on the same group, so don't send names or anything private.

#Milestones

Big projects fail in the middle, when nothing works and you can't tell which part is broken. Milestones stop that: each one adds a small piece, and you test it before moving on. The next lesson follows these five for the voting system.

Milestone Done when
M1: Roles and screens Each board can take its role and shows a distinct screen
M2: First message One message from the protocol travels and changes the other board's state
M3: Core job The main feature works end to end in the simulator
M4: Failure feedback Lost messages and silent devices produce a visible warning
M5: Data out Data is logged or streamed, exported as CSV, and charted

Check your understanding

2 questions

1In the voting protocol, why does each vote carry the voter's id as its value?

  • Radio messages have no address; every board in the group hears them.

  • If a receipt is lost and the voter resends, the id lets the teacher spot the repeat instead of counting it twice.

  • A value can be any number; the id is a design choice, not a rule of the radio.

Show answer

B. If a receipt is lost and the voter resends, the id lets the teacher spot the repeat instead of counting it twice.

2While drawing the voter's state diagram you realise there's no arrow out of Sent for "hears CLOSED". What should you do?

  • Every missing arrow is a question about behaviour. Answering it on paper is much cheaper than finding it as a bug.

  • A slow voter can be mid-retry when the teacher closes the poll.

  • Without Sent, the voter has no way to know whether to resend.

Show answer

A. Every missing arrow is a question about behaviour. Answering it on paper is much cheaper than finding it as a bug.

Key takeaways

  • The capstone needs roles, radio, events, states, data, failure feedback, testing, safety, and documentation.
  • Write the protocol table first: every message, its kind, who sends it, and what it means.
  • Draw a state diagram per role; every missing arrow is a question to answer before coding.
  • Plan the data from the question backwards, and fix column names now.
  • Split the build into milestones you can test one at a time.

What you'll learn

  • Start a multi-role project from a skeleton that matches the plan.
  • Add one feature per milestone and test it before moving on.
  • Count each voter once, even when messages are resent.
  • Give voters visible feedback when a vote is lost, using receipts, retries, and a timeout.
  • Export each poll's results and chart them.

This lesson builds the voting system from the planning lesson. Even if you chose a different idea, follow along: the five milestones, the role picker, the receipts, and the "draw only when something changed" loop carry straight over to any network you build. At the end there's a table showing how each milestone maps onto the other project ideas.

Here's one vote from start to finish, including the case the whole design is built around: a receipt that gets lost.

#The starter skeleton

Start every network project like this: all the variables from your plan, the radio group, and the role picker, with empty spots for each milestone. Paste it into the JavaScript view of a new MakeCode project.

Two things here are worth a look. myId = randint(1, 30000) gives each voter a random id when it starts, so the teacher can tell voters apart without names; two voters picking the same number is possible but rare in a class. And the forever loop builds a view string from everything the screen depends on, then calls draw() only when that string changes. The screen updates the moment the state changes, and the loop never wastes time redrawing an unchanged picture.

#Milestone 1: Roles and screens

Fill in draw() with one picture per role and state. Choosing pictures now makes every later test easier, because you can read a board's state off its face.

Test M1. Press A on the top board: a sleeping face (a voter, waiting). Press B on the bottom board: = (a teacher with no results yet). Both boards answered the role picker, and each shows its state. Done.

#Milestone 2: Open and close the poll

The teacher's A and B now open and close polls. Opening resets the tallies and the list of ids that have voted. Voters listen for the two strings.

Closing goes in the teacher's B branch: else if (role == "TEACHER" && state == "OPEN") { state = "CLOSED"; radio.sendString("CLOSED") }. Notice that CLOSED sends a voter to Waiting from any state, which answers the planning lesson's question about a vote still being resent when the poll ends.

Test M2. Teacher presses A: the teacher shows 0 and the voter's face changes to a target. Teacher presses B: the teacher shows =, the voter goes back to sleep.

#Milestone 3: Votes and the tally

A voter's A or B sends a vote whose value is its id. Both buttons do the same thing with a different letter, so they share a function:

In the voter branches of the button handlers, call castVote("A") and castVote("B"). The teacher counts a vote only the first time it sees an id:

voted.indexOf(value) < 0 means "this id isn't in the list yet". That one check is the difference between a fair vote and one where a stuck button or a resend counts twice.

Test M3. Open a poll, press B on the voter, close the poll. The teacher shows B. Open a new poll and press A on the voter three times in a row: the teacher's count stays at 1, because the voter left Voting after the first press.

#Milestone 4: Receipts and retries

Without a receipt, the voter's arrow stays up forever and nobody knows whether the vote counted. The teacher now acknowledges every vote it hears (even repeats, since a repeat means the voter missed the first ack), and the voter waits for an ack carrying its own id. Add the ack line at the end of the teacher's branch, and a voter branch:

The forever loop handles the timeout. If no receipt has come by retryAt, resend, up to three tries in total:

Why the randint(0, 500) in retryAt? Imagine 25 voters whose votes collided in the air at the same instant. If they all retried after exactly one second, they'd collide again. A random extra wait spreads the retries out so most get through on the second try.

Test M4. A vote now shows an arrow, then a tick. To test the failure path, put // in front of radio.sendValue("ack", value) and vote again: the arrow stays up for a few seconds while the voter retries, then turns into a cross. Press A or B on the cross to try again. Remove the // when you're done, and check that the tally still says 1 after all those retries.

#Milestone 5: Results out

When the teacher closes a poll, it streams the result over serial and writes one row to the data log, with the column names from the plan. Set the log up when the board becomes the teacher, so voter boards never touch the log:

Test M5. Run two polls in the simulator, then click Show data: you'll see the A and B values from each poll. On a real V2 teacher board, MY_DATA has one row per poll.

#The finished program

#Chart a week of polls

Here's what the teacher's log might hold after a week of one poll a day on "Should we have music during practice time? A = yes, B = no". The first cell saves the CSV; the second charts it.

The class swung from 39% yes to 73% yes over the week, and turnout crept up too. Because the log has a voters column, you can check the numbers: A plus B always equals voters, so no vote was counted twice or lost after it was acknowledged.

#Mapping the milestones onto other projects

Milestone Relay race timer Climate network Sound monitor
M1 Roles and screens start gate, finish gate station number, hub zone number, display
M2 First message GO from start to finish one reading reaches the hub one level reaches the display
M3 Core job finish gate times the run with its own clock hub tracks every station display shows the loudest zone, averaged
M4 Failure feedback finish gate replies; start gate shows a cross if no reply per-station "last heard" zone goes grey if silent
M5 Data out lap times to the log readings to the log levels per zone to the log

Check your understanding

3 questions

1The teacher sends an ack even when it has already counted that id. Why?

  • The indexOf check makes sure it isn't counted again.

  • Acknowledging repeats is safe because counting is guarded separately by the list of ids.

  • The radio never requires an answer; this is a rule of your protocol.

Show answer

B. Acknowledging repeats is safe because counting is guarded separately by the list of ids.

2You remove randint(0, 500) from retryAt, so every retry happens exactly one second later. When does that matter?

  • Two boards sending at the same instant can garble each other's packets.

  • The random extra wait spreads the retries out, which is why many networks use a random back-off.

  • The simulator rarely loses packets at all; collisions are a real-hardware, many-board problem.

Show answer

B. The random extra wait spreads the retries out, which is why many networks use a random back-off.

3Why does the forever loop compare view with shown before calling draw()?

  • showIcon and showNumber take time to display. Redrawing an unchanged picture every pass would slow the timeout checks.

  • It's an ordinary function and can be called any number of times.

  • The voter's state and the teacher's id list handle that.

Show answer

A. showIcon and showNumber take time to display. Redrawing an unchanged picture every pass would slow the timeout checks.

Key takeaways

  • Start from a skeleton that already holds the plan: variables, group, roles, and empty milestone spots.
  • Test each milestone before starting the next, including the "nothing should happen" cases.
  • A unique id per sender lets the receiver ignore repeats and address receipts.
  • Receipts, a timeout, and a few retries with a random wait turn lost messages into visible, recoverable failures.
  • Log one row per meaningful event, with columns you can cross-check later.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Three or four options: use the logo touch (input.onLogoEvent) or A+B as extra choices, and add columns to the log.
  • Let the teacher see turnout live: plot voted.length against the class size as a bar graph while the poll is open.
  • Anonymous results screen: a third role that only hears CLOSED and the teacher's results message, for projecting on the board.

#Further reading

  • Remote data collection (opens in a new tab): more on hubs and stations, including identifying senders with radio.setTransmitSerialNumber.
  • MakeCode radio reference (opens in a new tab): the full list of send, receive, and packet blocks, for adapting the protocol to your project.

m8-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write a test plan that covers normal use, edge cases, failures, and scale.
  • Measure how reliable your radio link is and chart the result.
  • Track down a silent board with a step-by-step checklist.
  • Document the invention so someone else could build it, including safety notes.
  • Present a short demo and assess your work against the rubric.

Your network works on your desk. Then you carry the teacher board to the front of a real classroom, twenty-five people press buttons in the same second, and three of them see crosses. That isn't failure; that's what testing is for. A project that has been tested shows you exactly where it breaks, which is far more useful than one that's never been pushed.

#Write the test plan before you test

A test plan is a table of things to try, each with the result you expect before you try it. Writing the expected result first stops you from deciding afterwards that whatever happened was fine. Cover four kinds of test:

  • Normal use: the main job, done the way you intended.
  • Edge cases: legal but unusual actions, like pressing buttons twice or at the wrong moment.
  • Failures: something goes wrong on purpose, like a lost message or a board out of range.
  • Scale: more devices, more messages, or a longer run than your desk test.

Here's a plan for the voting network. Make yours the same shape, and fill in the last column as you go.

# Kind Do this Expect Result
1 normal Open poll, vote A, close Teacher shows A; log row 1, 0, 1
2 edge Vote before the poll opens Voter stays asleep; nothing counted
3 edge Press A three times while voting Counted once
4 edge Close the poll while a vote is retrying Voter returns to sleep, no cross
5 failure Disable the ack line, then vote Arrow, retries, then a cross
6 failure Teacher out of range (real boards) Cross after about 3 to 5 seconds
7 scale 10+ real voters vote at once Every voter gets a tick within 5 s
8 scale Two classes on groups 31 and 32 Neither poll counts the other's votes

Tests 6 to 8 need real boards. If you're simulator-only, say so in your documentation and explain what you'd expect; a clear "not tested, and here's why" is better than silence.

#Measure reliability, don't guess it

"It works from across the room" is an opinion. "19 of 20 messages arrived at 20 metres" is a measurement. To test range, put a sender at one end of a corridor and a receiver that counts messages at the other. Send 20 numbered messages at each distance and record how many arrived. Here's the sort of log one test might produce, charted:

The dashed line marks a 90% target. In this example the link is solid up to 20 metres and falls apart past 30, so a voting network in one classroom is safe, and one spread across a building isn't. Your numbers will differ with walls, bodies, and transmit power, which is exactly why you measure your own. Record where you tested (corridor, open field, through a door) next to the numbers.

#When a board stays silent

Radio bugs rarely crash; the receiver just does nothing. Work through the checks in order, because each one is quicker than the next:

The last step is your general-purpose tool. serial.writeLine("got " + name + " " + value) at the top of a receive handler shows every message in the Show data console, so you can see whether it arrived and what it really contained. Delete the debug lines once the bug is fixed.

#Document it so someone else could build it

Your documentation is a README: one page that lets a classmate rebuild and use your network without asking you anything. Use this outline:

The "known problems" line matters. Every real project has limits, and stating them shows you understand your design.

#Safety notes worth copying

Pick the ones that apply and put them in your README's Safety section:

  • Power each board only from its USB cable or its own battery pack; hold boards by the edges.
  • Don't mix old and new batteries, and keep loose wires and clips from touching both battery terminals.
  • Keep electronics clear of water. If a board gets wet, unplug it and let it dry fully before use.
  • Never connect anything in the project to mains power.
  • Radio is readable by anyone on your group: don't send names, passwords, or private information.
  • For anything worn or carried while moving, secure cables and boards so nothing snags or trips.

#Present it in three minutes

A good demo is short and shows the hard part working. This shape fits in three minutes:

  1. The problem (20 seconds): who has it and why it matters. "Hand-count votes get miscounted and nobody can check."
  2. The normal case (60 seconds): run it live in the simulator or on real boards.
  3. The failure case (40 seconds): break something on purpose and show the feedback. This is the part audiences remember.
  4. The data (30 seconds): one chart and what it tells you.
  5. What's next (30 seconds): your top improvement and the limit it would fix.

Practise once with a timer. Have a recorded backup (a screen recording of the simulator) in case the live demo misbehaves.

#Rubric

Criterion Getting there Solid Excellent
Works as specified Main job works sometimes Main job works reliably in tests Works reliably, including edge cases in the plan
Radio protocol Messages work but aren't documented Protocol table matches the code Table matches code; every important message has a reply
Events and states Some polling; states unclear Events for inputs; one state machine with a diagram Every role has a diagram that matches its code exactly
Failure feedback None Lost messages or silent devices are shown Shown and recoverable (retry, re-join)
Data and analysis Data recorded but not used CSV exported and charted Chart answers the planned question, with a stated conclusion
Testing A few informal tries Test plan with expected and actual results Plan covers all four kinds; reliability measured
Documentation and safety Partial README Complete README with safety notes Someone else rebuilt it from the README alone
Presentation Over time or no demo Clear demo of the normal case Normal case, failure case, and data in three minutes

#Reflect

Write a short answer to each question at the end of your README:

  • Which bug took longest to find, and which step of the silent-board checklist would have found it faster?
  • Where did your state diagram and your code disagree, and which one was right?
  • What did your data show that you didn't expect?

#Where to go next

You've built a network of devices that sense, decide, talk, and record. Some directions from here:

  • Go deeper in MicroPython at python.microbit.org. Rebuild your network in Python, with the log module for data logging and radio.receive_full() for signal strength and timing.
  • Train a model on movement with micro:bit CreateAI, then use its output as an event in a MakeCode program.
  • Browse real projects in the micro:bit "Make it: code it" collection for sensors, radio, and data logging ideas you can extend.

#Further reading

  • micro:bit CreateAI (opens in a new tab): the free browser tool for training movement models and using them in MakeCode.
  • Make it: code it projects (opens in a new tab): the Micro:bit Educational Foundation's project library, filterable by feature and difficulty.
  • micro:bit Python Editor (opens in a new tab): the editor and simulator for taking your network into MicroPython.
